questions.stem: A 35-year-old male presents to the emergency department after an accidental chemical exposure to his eyes while working in a lab. He reports immediate burning and decreased vision. Upon examination, there is corneal epithelial loss and conjunctival swelling. What is the most appropriate immediate management step?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male presents to the emergency department after an accidental chemical exposure to his eyes while working in a lab. He reports immediate burning and decreased vision. Upon examination, there is corneal epithelial loss and conjunctival swelling. What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.label: A
options.text: Necrotic tissue removal and administer topical antibiotics

options.label: C
options.text: Immediate irrigation with water or saline for 20-30 minutes

questions.answerText: Immediate irrigation with water or saline for 20-30 minutes
questions.solution: /strong> Explanation: The above clinical case is suggestive of chemical injury. Irrigation with water or saline is the priority to dilute and remove the chemical, minimizing damage. Management of Chemical Injury Immediate irrigation: Copious water/saline for 20–30 min or until pH normal; double eversion of lids. Debridement: Removal of dead conjunctiva/corneal epithelium with cotton swab ( Option A ). Antibiotics: To prevent secondary infection ( Option A ). Cycloplegics: For ciliary muscle relaxation and pain relief. Steroids: Only for initial 7 days (reduce inflammation but impair healing) ( Option B ). Vitamin C (Ascorbic acid): 10% eye drops 2-hourly to promote collagen synthesis. Collagenase inhibitors: Citrate 10% drops, tetracycline, acetylcysteine 10%. Early surgical options: Tenon advancement, limbal cell transplant, amniotic membrane graft. Late surgical options: Symblepharon release with conjunctival/mucous graft, keratoplasty ( Option D ). if corneal opacity. Complications: Secondary glaucoma, limbal stem cell deficiency, pseudopterygium, corneal opacity @Neet_pg_bot

Explanation:

The above clinical case is suggestive of chemical injury. Irrigation with water or saline is the priority to dilute and remove the chemical, minimizing damage.

Management of Chemical Injury

  • Immediate irrigation: Copious water/saline for 20–30 min or until pH normal; double eversion of lids.
  • Debridement: Removal of dead conjunctiva/corneal epithelium with cotton swab (Option A).
  • Antibiotics: To prevent secondary infection (Option A).
  • Cycloplegics: For ciliary muscle relaxation and pain relief.Steroids: Only for initial 7 days (reduce inflammation but impair healing) (Option B).
  • Vitamin C (Ascorbic acid): 10% eye drops 2-hourly to promote collagen synthesis.
  • Collagenase inhibitors: Citrate 10% drops, tetracycline, acetylcysteine 10%.
  • Early surgical options: Tenon advancement, limbal cell transplant, amniotic membrane graft.
  • Late surgical options: Symblepharon release with conjunctival/mucous graft, keratoplasty (Option D). if corneal opacity.

Complications: Secondary glaucoma, limbal stem cell deficiency, pseudopterygium, corneal opacity

questions.stemHtml: A 36-year-old male presents to the clinic with complaints of bilateral cataracts, short stature, premature greying and loss of hair, and skin changes. He also reports joint stiffness and pain, as well as type 2 diabetes mellitus. On examination, the patient appears older than his stated age, with characteristic "bird-like" facies and a high-pitched voice. Which of the following conditions is most likely to be associated with his presentation?
questions.solution: inical presentation points towards Werner syndrome, also known as Adult Progeria Syndrome , an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by premature ageing features that typically manifest in adulthood . It is associated with a DNA helicase defect. Patients with Werner Syndrome are typically present in their third decade of life with symptoms of accelerated ageing. Clinically present with premature ageing features, including bilateral cataracts, short stature, premature greying and loss of hair, skin changes, joint stiffness and pain, and metabolic abnormalities such as type 2 diabetes mellitus. The characteristic "bird-like" facies and high-pitched voice are distinctive features of Werner Syndrome. Genetic mutation: WRN gene . [WRN = Werner syndrome gene (on chromosome 8)]. {{caption_text}} Hutchinson-Gilford Syndrome (Option A): It is a rare genetic progeroid syndrome characterized by severe premature ageing features that begin in childhood . It is a Laminopathy due to a Lamin-A (LMNA) gene mutation. Wermer Syndrome (Option C): Wermer Syndrome is for as multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1). Cockayne Syndrome (Option D): It is also a rare autosomal recessive progeroid syndrome. However, it typically presents in childhood. ERCC gene defect. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: D

Aspiration is the most common cause of lung abscesses , particularly in the apical lower lobe, and is frequently associated with anaerobic bacteria from the oral cavity. Lung Abscess Localized suppuration in the lung is characterized by tissue necrosis Aetiology: Infectious: Pneumonia due to Streptococcus, Pneumococcus, Haemophilus, Staphylococcus, anaerobic bacteria, etc. Chronic upper respiratory infections (e.g., sinusitis, tonsillitis, dental infections). Mechanical: Bronchial obstruction due to tumours or foreign bodies. Other Causes: Septicaemia and aspiration, commonly lead to lung abscess in the apical lower lobe. Sites of Infection: Apical Lower Lobe: Most frequently involved in aspiration-related lung abscesses. Posterior Segments: Can be affected due to gravity when aspiration occurs. Upper Lobes: May be involved in cases of tuberculosis or certain types of pneumonia. Routes of Infection: Aspiration: Inhalation of oropharyngeal or gastrointestinal secretions, often leading to anaerobic infections from the oral cavity. Hematogenous Spread: From e.g., endocarditis or septicemia Direct Extension: Localized infections in adjacent structures (e.g., pneumonia, empyema) can extend into lung tissue. Hematogenous spread from endocarditis (Option B) : While it can cause lung abscesses, it is less common than aspiration in the context of anaerobic infections and would typically present with multiple abscesses rather than a localized opacity. Direct extension from pneumonia (Option C) can cause lung abscesses, but in this case, the specific presence of anaerobic bacteria and the apical location suggest aspiration as the more likely cause. questions.solutionHtml:
tion:

The X-ray shows a lung abscess. Aspiration is the most common cause of lung abscesses, particularly in the apical lower lobe, and is frequently associated with anaerobic bacteria from the oral cavity.

 

Lung Abscess Localized suppuration in the lung is characterized by tissue necrosis

 

Aetiology:

  • Infectious: Pneumonia due to Streptococcus, Pneumococcus, Haemophilus, Staphylococcus, anaerobic bacteria, etc.
  • Chronic upper respiratory infections (e.g., sinusitis, tonsillitis, dental infections).
  • Mechanical: Bronchial obstruction due to tumours or foreign bodies.
  • Other Causes: Septicaemia and aspiration, commonly lead to lung abscess in the apical lower lobe.

Sites of Infection:

  • Apical Lower Lobe: Most frequently involved in aspiration-related lung abscesses.
  • Posterior Segments: Can be affected due to gravity when aspiration occurs.
  • Upper Lobes: May be involved in cases of tuberculosis or certain types of pneumonia.

 

Routes of Infection:

  • Aspiration: Inhalation of oropharyngeal or gastrointestinal secretions, often leading to anaerobic infections from the oral cavity.
  • Hematogenous Spread: From e.g., endocarditis or septicemia
  • Direct Extension: Localized infections in adjacent structures (e.g., pneumonia, empyema) can extend into lung tissue.

 

 

Hematogenous spread from endocarditis (Option B): While it can cause lung abscesses, it is less common than aspiration in the context of anaerobic infections and would typically present with multiple abscesses rather than a localized opacity.

Direct extension from pneumonia (Option C) can cause lung abscesses, but in this case, the specific presence of anaerobic bacteria and the apical location suggest aspiration as the more likely cause.

Bronchial obstruction due to lung cancer (Option D) is a possible cause of infection and abscess formation, but the presence of anaerobic bacteria and the patient's age make aspiration a more plausible cause, especially in the context of a localized opacity in the lung.

questions.stem: A mother brings her apparently normal 20-day-old newborn to the pediatric clinic with a complaint of milk coming through the nasal passages of the baby during feeding. Upon examination, you find the following: This condition is due to the failure of which of the following processes during embryonic development?
questions.stemHtml: A mother brings her apparently normal 20-day-old newborn to the pediatric clinic with a complaint of milk coming through the nasal passages of the baby during feeding. Upon examination, you find the following: This condition is due to the failure of which of the following processes during embryonic development?

options.label: A
options.text: Fusion of the maxillary and medial nasal processes

options.label: B
options.text: Formation of the lateral palatine processes

questions.solution: elves. Explanation: Cleft palate occurs when the palatal shelves fail to elevate and fuse properly during embryonic development, typically between the 6th and 9th weeks of gestation. This results in a gap in the palate, allowing communication between the oral and nasal cavities, as evidenced by milk coming through the nasal passages during feeding. Cleft palate: Defective fusion of the various components of the palate gives rise to clefts in the palate. Complete cleft palate: Bilateral complete cleft (A): Failure of fusion of both palatine processes of maxilla with premaxilla. A y-shaped cleft will be present between primary and secondary palate and between the two halves of secondary palate. It presents as a bilateral cleft of the upper lip also. Unilateral complete cleft (B): Nonfusion of one side palatine process of maxilla with premaxilla. It presents as a unilateral cleft of the upper lip. Incomplete cleft palate: Cleft of hard and soft palate( C): Cleft limited to hard palate. Cleft of soft palate (D): Cleft limited to hard palate. Bifid uvula (E): Cleft limited to uvula. Fusion of the maxillary and medial nasal processes (Option A): This contributes to formation of the upper lip and primary palate . Its failure leads to cleft lip , not cleft palate. Formation of the lateral palatine processes (Option B): While formation is important, fusion failure (not formation) is responsible for the defect in this case. Formation of the primary palate (Option D): The primary palate forms the region anterior to the incisive foramen; its failure causes anterior clefting , not posterior palatal clefts. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
elves.

 

Explanation:

 

  • Cleft palate occurs when the palatal shelves fail to elevate and fuse properly during embryonic development, typically between the 6th and 9th weeks of gestation.
  • This results in a gap in the palate, allowing communication between the oral and nasal cavities, as evidenced by milk coming through the nasal passages during feeding.

Cleft palate:

Defective fusion of the various components of the palate gives rise to clefts in the palate.

 

Complete cleft palate:

  • Bilateral complete cleft (A): Failure of fusion of both palatine processes of maxilla with premaxilla. A y-shaped cleft will be present between primary and secondary palate and between the two halves of secondary palate. It presents as a bilateral cleft of the upper lip also.
  • Unilateral complete cleft (B): Nonfusion of one side palatine process of maxilla with premaxilla. It presents as a unilateral cleft of the upper lip.

 

Incomplete cleft palate:

  • Cleft of hard and soft palate( C): Cleft limited to hard palate.
  • Cleft of soft palate (D): Cleft limited to hard palate.
  • Bifid uvula (E): Cleft limited to uvula.

 

Fusion of the maxillary and medial nasal processes (Option A): This contributes to formation of the upper lip and primary palate. Its failure leads to cleft lip, not cleft palate.

Formation of the lateral palatine processes (Option B): While formation is important, fusion failure (not formation) is responsible for the defect in this case.

Formation of the primary palate (Option D): The primary palate forms the region anterior to the incisive foramen; its failure causes anterior clefting, not posterior palatal clefts.

questions.stem: A 45 y/o male undergoes abdominal surgery and requires fluid replacement. The patient has a history of chronic kidney disease. Which of the following fluids is most appropriate for maintenance during surgery to avoid the risk of hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 45 y/o male undergoes abdominal surgery and requires fluid replacement. The patient has a history of chronic kidney disease. Which of the following fluids is most appropriate for maintenance during surgery to avoid the risk of hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis?
questions.solution: 's Lactate is often preferred because it contains a buffer (lactate) that helps to mitigate the risk of acidosis. It is isotonic and provides electrolytes in a more balanced way, making it a suitable option for patients with CKD. Ringer's Lactate (Balanced Crystalloid) Usage : Maintenance fluid during surgery. Advantage : Prevents hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, unlike normal saline. Excretion : Rapid elimination due to suppression of ADH secretion, promoting diuresis. Buffer : Lactate metabolised to bicarbonate, maintaining or slightly increasing HCO3− levels, hence preventing acidosis. ½ NS (0.45% NaCl, Hypotonic Saline) Usage : Maintenance fluid in the postoperative period along with 4% dextrose. Risk : To minimize the risk of hyponatremia, excessive use of hypotonic solutions, particularly in the postoperative phase, is discouraged. 3% NS (3% NaCl, Hypertonic Saline) Usage : Treatment of symptomatic hyponatremia and cerebral oedema. Mechanism : Draws water from intracellular to extracellular compartments, aiding in plasma volume expansion. Caution : Careful electrolyte and osmolality monitoring is required to avoid complications like osmotic demyelination. There is also a potential to cause fluid overload and hypernatremia, not recommended as a maintenance fluid. (Option C) 0.9% Normal Saline (Option A) : It may lead to hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis due to its high chloride content. 5% Dextrose in Water (Option D) : This hypotonic solution is used primarily for free water replacement, not surgical maintenance. It is usually used perioperatively and must be avoided in the postoperative period as it can severely dilute plasma electrolytes and osmolality. Note: An isotonic solution in the postoperative period could lead to potential GI dysfunction, when administered in excess, due to increased mucosal edema. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
's Lactate is often preferred because it contains a buffer (lactate) that helps to mitigate the risk of acidosis.
  • It is isotonic and provides electrolytes in a more balanced way, making it a suitable option for patients with CKD.

    •  

    Ringer's Lactate (Balanced Crystalloid)

    • Usage: Maintenance fluid during surgery.
    • Advantage: Prevents hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, unlike normal saline.
    • Excretion:
      • Rapid elimination due to suppression of ADH secretion, promoting diuresis.

    • Buffer: Lactate metabolised to bicarbonate, maintaining or slightly increasing HCO3− levels, hence preventing acidosis.

     

    ½ NS (0.45% NaCl, Hypotonic Saline)

    • Usage: Maintenance fluid in the postoperative period along with 4% dextrose.
    • Risk: To minimize the risk of hyponatremia, excessive use of hypotonic solutions, particularly in the postoperative phase, is discouraged.

    3% NS (3% NaCl, Hypertonic Saline)

    • Usage: Treatment of symptomatic hyponatremia and cerebral oedema.
    • Mechanism: Draws water from intracellular to extracellular compartments, aiding in plasma volume expansion.
    • Caution: Careful electrolyte and osmolality monitoring is required to avoid complications like osmotic demyelination. There is also a potential to cause fluid overload and hypernatremia, not recommended as a maintenance fluid. (Option C)

    0.9% Normal Saline (Option A): It may lead to hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis due to its high chloride content.

    5% Dextrose in Water (Option D):

    • This hypotonic solution is used primarily for free water replacement, not surgical maintenance.
    • It is usually used perioperatively and must be avoided in the postoperative period as it can severely dilute plasma electrolytes and osmolality.

questions.stemHtml: A 68-year-old male presents to the clinic with worsening dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, and ankle swelling. He has a past medical history of chronic heart failure, which was diagnosed 5 years ago. Despite being on several medications, he continues to experience symptoms. On examination, his heart rate is irregular and there is evidence of jugular venous distension. What is the drug of choice for managing his condition?
questions.solution: cardiac glycoside, is commonly used to manage chronic heart failure with atrial fibrillation and rapid ventricular response. It helps control heart rate and improve symptoms in patients with atrial fibrillation. Digoxin at therapeutic concentrations mildly inhibits the cardiac Na + /K + ATPase, causing an increase in intracellular Na + . Increased Na + inhibits Ca 2+ extrusion via the NCX, resulting in higher intracellular Ca 2+ and enhanced contractility. The increased contractility and cardiac output provide symptomatic relief (primarily in systolic dysfunction) in patients with heart failure. When the main trigger for neurohumoral activation is removed, sympathetic nerve tone, heart rate, and peripheral vascular resistance drop. The decrease in preload and afterload reduces chamber dilation and wall stress. Increased renal perfusion lowers renin production and increases diuresis, further decreasing preload. Lisinopril (Option A) is an ACE inhibitor used in heart failure, but does not directly address the patient's atrial fibrillation or rapid ventricular response. Carvedilol (Option B) is a beta-blocker used in heart failure but does not specifically target atrial fibrillation. Furosemide (Option C) is a loop diuretic that manages fluid overload in heart failure but does not address the patient's arrhythmia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Conn's syndrome, also known as primary hyperaldosteronism, which is due to autonomous overproduction of aldosterone, usually from an adrenal adenoma. It is characterised by resistant hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Causes: Aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn's adenoma) - Most common. Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. Symptoms often include muscle weakness, fatigue, headaches, and frequent urination. Laboratory findings: Elevated plasma aldosterone levels Suppressed plasma renin activity High aldosterone-to-renin ratio Treatment involves surgical removal of the adenoma and the use of mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, such as spironolactone and eplerenone. Role of Aldosterone : It acts on the collecting duct to – Increase sodium reabsorption via epithelial sodium channels (ENaC). Enhance potassium secretion through potassium channels (ROMK). Bartter's syndrome(Option A) It is a genetic disorder,childhood-onset, affecting the kidneys, leading to abnormalities in electrolyte reabsorption. Typically presents with low blood pressure, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, elevated renin levels, and high urinary calcium excretion (hypercalciuria). Gitelman's syndrome :( Option B) A genetic disorder affects the distal convoluted tubule of the kidney, leading to hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Typically presents with low or normal blood pressure and low urinary calcium excretion (hypocalciuria). Liddle's syndrome(Option D) It is a genetic disorder caused by the increased activity of epithelial sodium channels (ENaC), leading to sodium retention and potassium excretion. It has low aldosterone and renin levels and typically presents with hypertension. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Conn's syndrome, also known as primary hyperaldosteronism, which is due to autonomous overproduction of aldosterone, usually from an adrenal adenoma.
  • It is characterised by resistant hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis.
  • Causes:
    • Aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn's adenoma) - Most common.
    • Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia.
  • Symptoms often include muscle weakness, fatigue, headaches, and frequent urination.
  • Laboratory findings:
    • Elevated plasma aldosterone levels
    • Suppressed plasma renin activity
    • High aldosterone-to-renin ratio
  • Treatment involves surgical removal of the adenoma and the use of mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, such as spironolactone and eplerenone.

Role of Aldosterone: It acts on the collecting duct to –

  • Increase sodium reabsorption via epithelial sodium channels (ENaC).
  • Enhance potassium secretion through potassium channels (ROMK).

Bartter's syndrome(Option A)

  • It is a genetic disorder,childhood-onset, affecting the kidneys, leading to abnormalities in electrolyte reabsorption.
  • Typically presents with low blood pressure, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, elevated renin levels, and high urinary calcium excretion (hypercalciuria).

Gitelman's syndrome:(Option B)

  • A genetic disorder affects the distal convoluted tubule of the kidney, leading to hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and metabolic alkalosis.
  • Typically presents with low or normal blood pressure and low urinary calcium excretion (hypocalciuria).

Liddle's syndrome(Option D)

  • It is a genetic disorder caused by the increased activity of epithelial sodium channels (ENaC), leading to sodium retention and potassium excretion.
  • It has low aldosterone and renin levels and typically presents with hypertension.

Oral Tendencies : A tendency to put objects in their mouth, even those that are not edible. Hypersexuality : An increased and often inappropriate sexual drive. Cerebellum (Option A): Responsible for motor coordination and balance . Damage → ataxia , dysmetria, intention tremor. Does not cause behavioral symptoms like hypersexuality or hyperorality. Hippocampus (Option C): Critical for forming new memories . Damage → anterograde amnesia . Does not cause hypersexuality or placidity . questions.stem: During the third week of gestation, the formation of the primitive streak signifies the start of gastrulation. Which statement about the primitive streak accurately describes this process?
questions.stemHtml: During the third week of gestation, the formation of the primitive streak signifies the start of gastrulation. Which statement about the primitive streak accurately describes this process?

options.label: A
options.text: It forms from hypoblast cells and establishes the embryonic central axis.

options.label: B
options.text: It appears dorsally, becoming linear and marking the transition to a trilaminar disc.

options.label: C
options.text: It develops into the prechordal plate, defining the head-tail axis.

options.label: D
options.text: It originates from trophoblast cells, contributing to the amniotic cavity and yolk sac formation.

questions.answerText: It appears dorsally, becoming linear and marking the transition to a trilaminar disc.
questions.solution: The primitive streak is a key structure that forms on the dorsal aspect of the embryonic disc and becomes a linear structure as the disc elongates. This marks the beginning of gastrulation and the transition from a bilaminar to a trilaminar disc , establishing the embryonic axis . The primitive streak is an early, temporary structure that emerges in the blastula during the initial stages of embryonic development. Around the 15th day of development, following the formation of the prechordal plate, epiblast cells along the central axis near the tail end of the embryo start to proliferate, creating an elevation that protrudes into the amniotic cavity known as the primitive streak . (Option A, B and D) Its cranial end forms the primitive node. A groove called a primitive groove appears in the primitive streak, which continues with a small depression, a primitive pit , in the primitive node. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
• The primitive streak is a key structure that forms on the dorsal aspect of the embryonic disc and becomes a linear structure as the disc elongates.
  • This marks the beginning of gastrulation and the transition from a bilaminar to a trilaminar disc, establishing the embryonic axis.

 

  • The primitive streak is an early, temporary structure that emerges in the blastula during the initial stages of embryonic development.
  • Around the 15th day of development, following the formation of the prechordal plate, epiblast cells along the central axis near the tail end of the embryo start to proliferate, creating an elevation that protrudes into the amniotic cavity known as the primitive streak. (Option A, B and D)
  • Its cranial end forms the primitive node.
  • A groove called a primitive groove appears in the primitive streak, which continues with a small depression, a primitive pit, in the primitive node.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female presents with a breast lump. On biopsy, the tissue shows anaplastic cells without any differentiation. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining is performed to characterise the tumour further. Which marker would be most appropriate to confirm the epithelial origin of the tumour cells in breast cancer?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old female presents with a breast lump. On biopsy, the tissue shows anaplastic cells without any differentiation. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining is performed to characterise the tumour further. Which marker would be most appropriate to confirm the epithelial origin of the tumour cells in breast cancer?
questions.solution: >) CK7 Explanation: In a female with a breast lump and presence of anaplastic cells, CK7 (cytokeratin 7) is the most appropriate marker to confirm the epithelial origin of the tumor, as cytokeratins are commonly expressed in all carcinomas. In I mmunohistochemistry (IHC) , a CK7 and CK20 profile is commonly used to help determine the tumor origin. Most female-origin cancers (breast, endometrial, thyroid, cervical) typically show a CK7-positive and CK20-negative pattern. (Option D) ER (estrogen receptor), PR (progesterone receptor), and HER2 (human epidermal growth factor receptor 2) are other markers that can be positive in breast cancer, which help in deciding management. CD20 (Option A) is a B-cell marker that is typically positive in B-cell lymphomas, including non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). Pp3 (Option B) is a marker positive in squamous cell carcinoma in the lung. TTF-1(thyroid transcription factor-1) (Option D) is a marker positive in the adenocarcinoma of the lung. @Neet_pg_bot

Explanation:

In a female with a breast lump and presence of anaplastic cells, CK7 (cytokeratin 7) is the most appropriate marker to confirm the epithelial origin of the tumor, as cytokeratins are commonly expressed in all carcinomas.

  • In Immunohistochemistry (IHC), a CK7 and CK20 profile is commonly used to help determine the tumor origin.

The patient’s heart rate is 110/min, blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management step based on the CVP and clinical findings?
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old male patient is undergoing major abdominal surgery under general anesthesia. After induction of anesthesia, the patient's CVP is measured at 3 cm H2O. The patient’s heart rate is 110/min, blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management step based on the CVP and clinical findings?
questions.solution: ata-dictid="ee07cb1aaf16927771856285b258d9">CVP (3 cm H2O) suggests hypovolemia , which is consistent with the patient's tachycardia and hypotension. Administering a fluid bolus is the first-line treatment to increase preload and improve hemodynamics. Central Venous Pressure (CVP) Monitoring: CVP measures the pressure in the thoracic vena cava near the right atrium, reflecting right ventricular preload and overall fluid status. Measurement Method (Invasive): Central venous catheter placed in large veins (e.g., subclavian or internal jugular), connected to a pressure transducer Normal Range: 3-8 mmHg. Low CVP Causes: Hypovolemia (blood loss or dehydration). Venodilation (e.g., in septic shock). Elevated CVP Causes: Heart failure, fluid overload, valve dysfunction. Increased intrathoracic pressure (e.g., mechanical ventilation, tension pneumothorax). Clinical Use: Guides fluid resuscitation. Helps assess heart function and venous return. Vasopressors (Option A) may be required if hypotension persists after adequate fluid resuscitation, but not as the initial step. Blood transfusion (Option C) is not indicated unless there is evidence of blood loss or anemia. Increasing anesthetic depth (Option D) is inappropriate here, as the patient is likely hypovolemic. @Neet_pg_bot

ata-dictid="ee07cb1aaf16927771856285b258d9">CVP (3 cm H2O) suggests hypovolemia, which is consistent with the patient's tachycardia and hypotension. Administering a fluid bolus is the first-line treatment to increase preload and improve hemodynamics.

 

Central Venous Pressure (CVP) Monitoring:

CVP measures the pressure in the thoracic vena cava near the right atrium, reflecting right ventricular preload and overall fluid status.

Measurement Method (Invasive):

Central venous catheter placed in large veins (e.g., subclavian or internal jugular), connected to a pressure transducer

Normal Range: 3-8 mmHg.

Low CVP Causes:

  • Hypovolemia (blood loss or dehydration).
  • Venodilation (e.g., in septic shock).

Elevated CVP Causes:

  • Heart failure, fluid overload, valve dysfunction.
  • Increased intrathoracic pressure (e.g., mechanical ventilation, tension pneumothorax).

Clinical Use:

  • Guides fluid resuscitation.
  • Helps assess heart function and venous return.

 

Vasopressors (Option A) may be required if hypotension persists after adequate fluid resuscitation, but not as the initial step.

Blood transfusion (Option C) is not indicated unless there is evidence of blood loss or anemia.

Increasing anesthetic depth (Option D) is inappropriate here, as the patient is likely hypovolemic.

Category

Exposure Type

Management

Category I

    • Human rabies Immunoglobulin or HRIG

  • Not needed for previously vaccinated individuals

Type of Cyst

Description

Details

Functional Cyst

Fluid-filled sacs that form on the ovaries, typically during the menstrual cycle.

  •  2 Types:
    1. Follicular cysts form due to hormonal dysfunction prior to ovulation, leading to expansion of the follicular antrum with serous fluid.
    2. Corpus luteum cysts form due to excessive hemorrhage from the vascular corpus luteum following ovulation.
  • High-dose combination oral contraceptives (COCs) suppress ovarian activity and protect against cyst development.
  • Surgical excision is considered for large, persistent cysts or smaller ones causing persistent symptoms. Usually benign and not cancerous.

Gartner’s Cyst

Forms from remnants of the Wolffian duct

  • Located along vaginal walls
  • Can cause discomfort, urinary issues, or dyspareunia if large
  • Treatment may involve surgical removal if symptomatic

Skene’s Cyst

Located near the urethra in females, formed from the Skene’s glands.

  • Involved in lubrication of the urethral opening. Usually presents as a urethral diverticulum.
  • Cysts here can cause urinary problems, pain, or discomfort.
  • Treatment may include antibiotics for infection or surgical drainage/removal if necessary.

Nabothian Cyst

Mucus-filled cysts that occur on the cervix.

  • Form when mucus-producing glands in the cervix are covered by skin cells, trapping the mucus.
  • Generally harmless, asymptomatic and often found during routine pelvic exams.
  • No treatment is typically required unless they cause significant symptoms, in which case they can be drained or removed.

se:collapse; width:624px">

Definition

Postpartum thyroiditis is an inflammation of the thyroid gland that occurs after childbirth, typically within the first year postpartum

Etiology

  • Autoimmune Factors
  • Genetic Predisposition
  • Hormonal Changes

Clinical manifestations

It has 2 phases which has a clinical progression-

Thyrotoxic phase( 1-4 months) (Option A)

Hypothyroid phase( 4 to 8 months) (Option B)

The hypothyroid phase either leads to euthyroid phase (Option C) or permanent hypothyroidism (Option D).

Investigation

Thyroid Function Tests:

  • TSH: Elevated in the hypothyroid phase, suppressed in the hyperthyroid phase.
  • Free T4: Elevated in the hyperthyroid phase, decreased in the hypothyroid phase.
  • Free T3: May also be elevated in the hyperthyroid phase.

Thyroid Antibodies:

  • Anti-thyroid Peroxidase (Anti-TPO) Antibodies: Often elevated, indicating an autoimmune component.

Treatment:

  1. Hyperthyroid phase- Beta blockers
  2. Hypothyroid phase- Levothyroxine, (25 mcg to 75 mcg)

Management

Criteria/Indication

Description

Expectant Management
  • Beta hCG < 1,500 IU/L
  • No significant symptoms
  • Strong likelihood of spontaneous resolution
  • Monitoring without intervention, relying on the natural resolution of the ectopic pregnancy

Medical Management
  • Beta hCG < 3,000 IU/L
  • Adnexal mass < 4 cm
  • No fetal cardiac activity
  • Hemodynamically stable
  • Methotrexate (single dose/ multi-dose regimen) (best)

Surgical Management
  • Beta hCG > 5,000 IU/L
  • Size of ectopic > 4 cm
  • Presence of cardiac activity
  • Linear Salpingostomy (best)
  • Resection Anastomosis

questions.answerText: Excessive use of vitamin D preparations and phosphate binders
questions.solution: >Adynamic bone disease is a type of CKD–mineral bone disorder characterized by low bone turnover due to markedly reduced osteoblast and osteoclast activity. The main cause is over-suppression of PTH , often iatrogenic. This occurs with: High-dose vitamin D analogs (calcitriol, alfacalcidol) → suppress PTH secretion Calcium-containing phosphate binders (e.g., calcium acetate, calcium carbonate) → induce hypercalcemia and further suppress PTH Net effect: bone becomes metabolically inactive, unable to remodel → fracture risk and vascular calcification increase . @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
>Adynamic bone disease is a type of CKD–mineral bone disorder characterized by low bone turnover due to markedly reduced osteoblast and osteoclast activity.

  • The main cause is over-suppression of PTH, often iatrogenic.

  • This occurs with:

    • High-dose vitamin D analogs (calcitriol, alfacalcidol) → suppress PTH secretion

    • Calcium-containing phosphate binders (e.g., calcium acetate, calcium carbonate) → induce hypercalcemia and further suppress PTH

  • Net effect: bone becomes metabolically inactive, unable to remodel → fracture risk and vascular calcification increase.

  • Osteons are cylindrical functional units of bone.

These features are characteristic of Long-Chain 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency. This condition affects fatty acid oxidation and can manifest in both the child and mother, particularly with AFLP during pregnancy. May also contribute to acute fatty liver during pregnancy 3-Ketoacyl-CoA Thiolase and HMG-CoA Lyase Deficiency: These deficiencies not only disrupt fatty acid oxidation but also affect the breakdown of leucine, a ketogenic amino acid. 1. Carnitine Deficiency: Common in preterm babies Cause : Inadequate biosynthesis or renal leakage. Hemolysis Pathophysiology : Impaired fatty acid oxidation→hypoglycemia & Lipid accumulation→muscular weakness (Option D ruled out) 2. Muscular Weakness due to the buildup of lipids in muscles Coma Fatty Liver Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy: Due to Long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency indicating a potential role of hormonal changes influencing enzyme activity. Neurological Symptoms: Defects impacting fatty acid oxidation, especially those also affecting the breakdown of leucine. Differential Diagnosis: DKA (Benedict+, Rothera+): This would present with high blood glucose and elevated ketone bodies, which is not the case here. Starvation ketosis (Benedict-, Rothera+): This can also cause non-ketotic hypoglycemia, but without the fatty liver findings. questions.solutionHtml:
Correct answer : Option B- Long-Chain 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency 

  • The scenario describes a child with severe fatigue, vomiting, nonketotic hypoglycemia, and fatty liver, alongside a maternal history of acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP).
  • These features are characteristic of Long-Chain 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency.
    • This condition affects fatty acid oxidation and can manifest in both the child and mother, particularly with AFLP during pregnancy.
  • Other deficiencies listed do not specifically present with this combination of symptoms and maternal history.

 

FATTY ACID OXIDATION DEFECTS

CONGENITAL DEFECTS

ACQUIRED DEFECTS

1. CPT-I Deficiency:

  • Site: Liver
  • Pathophysiology: Leading to decreased fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis, which can result in hypoglycemia (Option A ruled out)
 

2. CPT-II Deficiency:

  • Site: Primarily affecting skeletal muscle and potentially the liver in severe cases
 

3. Defects in β-oxidation Enzymes: 2 types:

 
  • Long and Short-Chain 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency: Can cause nonketotic hypoglycemia, coma, and fatty liver. May also contribute to acute fatty liver during pregnancy
 
  • 3-Ketoacyl-CoA Thiolase and HMG-CoA Lyase Deficiency: These deficiencies not only disrupt fatty acid oxidation but also affect the breakdown of leucine, a ketogenic amino acid.

1. Carnitine Deficiency:

  • Common in preterm babies
  • Cause:
    • Inadequate biosynthesis or renal leakage.
    • Hemolysis
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Impaired fatty acid oxidation→hypoglycemia & Lipid accumulation→muscular weakness (Option D ruled out)
 

2. Jamaican Vomiting Sickness:

 
  • Cause: Consuming unripe ackee fruit containing the toxin hypoglycin,
  • Pathophysiology: This condition inhibits medium- and short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, leading to hypoglycemia (Option C ruled out)

CLINICAL FEATURES
  • Hypoglycemia
  • Nonketotic Hypoglycemia
  • Lipid Accumulation
  • Dicarboxylic Aciduria
    • Marked by the excretion of C6—C10 ω-dicarboxylic acids and non-ketotic hypoglycemia
    • It arises from a lack of mitochondrial medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase.
  • Muscular Weakness due to the buildup of lipids in muscles
  • Coma
  • Fatty Liver
  • Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy: Due to Long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency indicating a potential role of hormonal changes influencing enzyme activity.
  • Neurological Symptoms: Defects impacting fatty acid oxidation, especially those also affecting the breakdown of leucine.

 

Differential Diagnosis:

  1. DKA (Benedict+, Rothera+): This would present with high blood glucose and elevated ketone bodies, which is not the case here.
  2. Starvation ketosis (Benedict-, Rothera+): This can also cause non-ketotic hypoglycemia, but without the fatty liver findings.
  3. Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD): This amino acid disorder can impact fatty acid oxidation and cause hypoglycemia, but would likely present with a different pattern of symptoms.
  4. Type 1 Glycogen Storage Disease: This can also lead to fasting hypoglycemia, but would not typically involve fatty liver changes

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male undergoes a split-thickness skin graft for a large wound on his leg. Three days postoperatively, the graft appears swollen with fluid accumulating underneath it. Which of the following complications is most likely?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male undergoes a split-thickness skin graft for a large wound on his leg. Three days postoperatively, the graft appears swollen with fluid accumulating underneath it. Which of the following complications is most likely?
questions.solution: ictid="84294069061692777198bdff94a950">seroma formation Explanation: In this scenario, the accumulation of fluid beneath the graft is indicative of hematoma or seroma formation. This complication can prevent proper adherence of the graft to the wound bed, leading to graft failure if not addressed promptly. Hematomas are collections of blood, while seromas are accumulations of clear fluid. Both can occur when there is inadequate hemostasis or when there is excessive movement or pressure on the graft site post-operatively. Complications of Skin Grafting: Graft Failure (Option A ruled out) : This occurs when the graft does not survive or integrate with the recipient site, due to poor vascularization or improper placement. It is not characterized by fluid accumulation beneath the graft. It can be prevented by ensuring good contact between the graft and the wound bed and avoiding movement or pressure on the graft. Infection (Option C ruled out) : Infection typically presents with redness, warmth, and pus rather than just fluid accumulation. Strict sterile techniques during surgery and the use of prophylactic antibiotics can help prevent infections. Hematoma or Seroma Formation (Option B) : Occur when blood or fluid collects under the graft. Proper hemostasis during surgery and the use of drains can prevent this issue. Poor Cosmetic Outcome (Option D ruled out) : If the graft does not match the recipient site's skin texture or thickness, or if it is not placed correctly, the cosmetic result may be unsatisfactory. Careful selection of graft thickness and meticulous placement can help achieve a better aesthetic outcome. @Neet_pg_bot

Complications of Skin Grafting:

  1. Graft Failure (Option A ruled out):

    • Proper hemostasis during surgery and the use of drains can prevent this issue.
  4. Poor Cosmetic Outcome (Option D ruled out): 
    • If the graft does not match the recipient site's skin texture or thickness, or if it is not placed correctly, the cosmetic result may be unsatisfactory.

questions.stem: A researcher is investigating the association between a new dietary supplement and the development of a rare type of cancer. The study includes 100 patients with the cancer and 100 healthy individuals. All of the following biases can occur in this type of study except?
questions.stemHtml: A researcher is investigating the association between a new dietary supplement and the development of a rare type of cancer. The study includes 100 patients with the cancer and 100 healthy individuals. All of the following biases can occur in this type of study except?
questions.solution: p> Explanation: Pygmalion Bias occurs when the researcher's expectations influence participant performance. This bias is irrelevant to case-control studies, which are retrospective and observational and more susceptible to biases like recall, selection, and ascertainment bias. Pygmalion Bias/ Rosenthal Effect: A phenomenon where higher researcher expectations increase participant performance or outcomes. Motivation is proportional to performance and gives an exaggerated response. Seen in experimental or educational settings. For example, increased motivation by teachers increases student performance. Recall Bias (Option A) occurs when participants do not accurately remember past events or experiences. It is common in case-control studies where cases might remember exposure more clearly than controls. Selection Bias (Option B) Happens when there is a systematic difference in characteristics between those selected for study and those not. It is possible that the cases and controls are not representative of the general population. Surveillance Bias or Ascertainment bias (Option C) Occurs when the disease or outcome is more likely to be identified in the exposed group because they are more closely monitored. This could occur if cases are more frequently monitored for dietary habits than controls. @Neet_pg_bot

p>Explanation:

Pygmalion Bias occurs when the researcher's expectations influence participant performance. This bias is irrelevant to case-control studies, which are retrospective and observational and more susceptible to biases like recall, selection, and ascertainment bias.

 

Pygmalion Bias/ Rosenthal Effect:

  • A phenomenon where higher researcher expectations increase participant performance or outcomes.
  • Motivation is proportional to performance and gives an exaggerated response.
  • Seen in experimental or educational settings.
  • For example, increased motivation by teachers increases student performance.

 

Recall Bias (Option A) occurs when participants do not accurately remember past events or experiences.

  • It is common in case-control studies where cases might remember exposure more clearly than controls.

 

Selection Bias (Option B)

  • Happens when there is a systematic difference in characteristics between those selected for study and those not.
  • It is possible that the cases and controls are not representative of the general population.

 

Surveillance Bias or Ascertainment bias (Option C)

  • Occurs when the disease or outcome is more likely to be identified in the exposed group because they are more closely monitored.
  • This could occur if cases are more frequently monitored for dietary habits than controls.

questions.solution: Pneumonia is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in acute measles and is the most likely immediate complication in this case, especially in an unvaccinated child. It primarily affects children and is transmitted through respiratory droplets or small-particle aerosols . questions.solution: der-top:1px solid #000000; vertical-align:top"> Hypocalcemia Due to decreased calcium absorption in the intestine. Secondary Hyperparathyroidism In response to low calcium levels, the parathyroid hormone (PTH) increases, which increases calcium reabsorption from bone and the kidneys. Elevated Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) Due to Increased bone turnover as a result of increased PTH. 25-hydroxy cholecalciferol Decreased. der-top:1px solid #000000; vertical-align:top">

Hypocalcemia

Due to decreased calcium absorption in the intestine.

Hypophosphatemia

Due to decreased phosphate absorption in the intestine and decreased reabsorption of phosphate in the kidneys.

Secondary Hyperparathyroidism

In response to low calcium levels, the parathyroid hormone (PTH) increases, which increases calcium reabsorption from bone and the kidneys.

Elevated Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)

Due to Increased bone turnover as a result of increased PTH.

25-hydroxy cholecalciferol

Decreased.

 

Prolonged secondary hyperparathyroidism can cause renal osteodystrophy, which may lead to pathological fractures.

Primary hyperparathyroidism (Option B) leads to excess PTH production, causing hypercalcemia.

Hypoparathyroidism (Option C) presents with low PTH and hypocalcemia. Hypothyroidism is commonly associated with vitamin D deficiency, potentially due to immune dysfunction and impacts on calcium metabolism

Chronic kidney disease (Option D) causes secondary hyperparathyroidism due to impaired phosphate excretion and low 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D levels, it is typically associated with hyperphosphatemia.

questions.solution: detection test Explanation: A rapid antigen detection test (NS1) is used to diagnose dengue fever within 5 days of onset of fever. Nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) has been used but has not resolved the episodes. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.stemHtml: A 27-week gestational-age preterm infant in the NICU experiences persistent apnea lasting over 20 seconds despite gentle tactile stimulation and supplemental oxygen. Nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) has been used but has not resolved the episodes. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP)

questions.solution: citrate Explanation: Caffeine is the treatment of choice for recurrent or persistent apnea of prematurity that does not respond to initial measures like tactile stimulation or nCPAP. It increases central respiratory drive, lowers the threshold for response to hypercapnia, enhances diaphragmatic contractility, and prevents diaphragmatic fatigue. Management of Apnea of Prematurity: For mild and intermittent episodes: Gentle tactile stimulation or provision of supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula is often sufficient. If apnea episodes are more frequent or prolonged, nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) or heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula (HHHFNC) can be used to maintain airway patency. For recurrent or persistent apnea: Methylxanthines (e.g., caffeine) are preferred because they effectively stimulate respiratory drive and reduce the incidence and severity of apnea. Caffeine aids in extubation and lowers Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) risk with fewer side effects than theophylline. It is safe for oral or intravenous use with a wide therapeutic window and minimal need for serum monitoring. Continuing nCPAP (Option A) is beneficial for managing obstructive or mixed apnea by maintaining airway patency but is less effective for central apnea. Since the apnea persists despite nCPAP, additional pharmacological intervention is needed. Initiate doxapram infusion (Option C): Doxapram is a respiratory stimulant but is less commonly used due to side effects and is typically considered only if methylxanthines are ineffective. Start low-dose theophylline (Option D): Theophylline is another methylxanthine but is less preferred than caffeine due to a shorter half-life and higher risk of side effects d/t narrow therapeutic range (5-15 microgram), such as tachycardia and feeding intolerance. @Neet_pg_bot

Management of Apnea of Prematurity:

  • For mild and intermittent episodes: Gentle tactile stimulation or provision of supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula is often sufficient.
  • If apnea episodes are more frequent or prolonged, nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) or heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula (HHHFNC) can be used to maintain airway patency.
  • For recurrent or persistent apnea:
    • Methylxanthines (e.g., caffeine) are preferred because they effectively stimulate respiratory drive and reduce the incidence and severity of apnea.
    • Caffeine aids in extubation and lowers Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) risk with fewer side effects than theophylline.
    • It is safe for oral or intravenous use with a wide therapeutic window and minimal need for serum monitoring.

 

Continuing nCPAP (Option A) is beneficial for managing obstructive or mixed apnea by maintaining airway patency but is less effective for central apnea. Since the apnea persists despite nCPAP, additional pharmacological intervention is needed.

 

Initiate doxapram infusion (Option C): Doxapram is a respiratory stimulant but is less commonly used due to side effects and is typically considered only if methylxanthines are ineffective.

 

Start low-dose theophylline (Option D): Theophylline is another methylxanthine but is less preferred than caffeine due to a shorter half-life and higher risk of side effects d/t narrow therapeutic range (5-15 microgram), such as tachycardia and feeding intolerance.

questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male reports a gradual decrease in vision in his left eye over the past two months, describing it as a "dimming" rather than a complete loss. He also has difficulty reading and seeing clearly. As per the image below, which test is most likely being conducted?
questions.solution: f optic nerve dysfunction and the image depicted above is describing RAPD (Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect) which is tested by swinging flashlight test. Swinging flashlight test: The swinging flashlight test is used to detect a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) , often seen with unilateral optic nerve lesions, even when visual acuity is normal. Procedure: Shine a bright flashlight on one pupil and observe its constriction. Quickly move the light to the contralateral pupil and observe the response. Repeat the process several times, alternating between the two eyes. Normal response: Both pupils constrict equally, and the pupil receiving the light remains tightly constricted. Abnormal response (RAPD): If there is a relative afferent pathway defect, the affected pupil will dilate when the light is moved from the normal eye to the abnormal eye. Significance: The presence of Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD) is an early indication of optic nerve disease, even when visual acuity appears normal. Causes: Optic neuritis Optic neuropathy Chiasmal compression Intraocular hemorrhage Central serous retinopathy Cystoid macular edema Retinal detachment Optic tract lesion Central or branch arterial occlusion Central or branch vein occlusion Anisometropic amblyopia Cataract Corneal scar Visual pathway damage Perimetry (Option B) measures and maps the visual field, assessing peripheral vision to detect defects or abnormalities. It aids in diagnosing eye conditions like glaucoma, retinal diseases, and neurological disorders affecting visual pathways. Tonometry (Option C) is a diagnostic test used in Glaucoma to measure intraocular pressure (IOP). The visual acuity test (Option D) measures the sharpness or clarity of a person's vision. It evaluates how well a person can see details at a specific distance, typically assessing the ability to read letters or symbols on Snellen’s chart. @Neet_pg_bot

Swinging flashlight test:

  • The swinging flashlight test is used to detect a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), often seen with unilateral optic nerve lesions, even when visual acuity is normal.

 

Procedure:

  1. Shine a bright flashlight on one pupil and observe its constriction.
  2. Quickly move the light to the contralateral pupil and observe the response.
  3. Repeat the process several times, alternating between the two eyes.


 

  • Normal response: Both pupils constrict equally, and the pupil receiving the light remains tightly constricted.
  • Abnormal response (RAPD): If there is a relative afferent pathway defect, the affected pupil will dilate when the light is moved from the normal eye to the abnormal eye.
  • Significance: The presence of Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD) is an early indication of optic nerve disease, even when visual acuity appears normal.

 

Causes:

 

  • Optic neuritis
  • Optic neuropathy
  • Chiasmal compression
  • Intraocular hemorrhage
  • Central serous retinopathy
  • Cystoid macular edema
  • Retinal detachment
  • Optic tract lesion
  • Central or branch arterial occlusion
  • Central or branch vein occlusion
  • Anisometropic amblyopia
  • Cataract
  • Corneal scar
  • Visual pathway damage



 

Perimetry (Option B) measures and maps the visual field, assessing peripheral vision to detect defects or abnormalities.

  • It aids in diagnosing eye conditions like glaucoma, retinal diseases, and neurological disorders affecting visual pathways.

 

Tonometry (Option C) is a diagnostic test used in Glaucoma to measure intraocular pressure (IOP).

 

The visual acuity test (Option D) measures the sharpness or clarity of a person's vision.

  • It evaluates how well a person can see details at a specific distance, typically assessing the ability to read letters or symbols on Snellen’s chart.

Hormones of Spermatogenesis: Follicular stimulating hormone: FSH is essential for the initial development of spermatogonia cells. questions.solutionHtml:

The most plausible explanation for the observed hormonal imbalances and clinical features is a compromised ability of Sertoli cells to respond to FSH stimulation, leading to both impaired spermatogenesis and, consequently, low testosterone levels. The reduced negative feedback from inhibin due to impaired Sertoli cell function further contributes to the elevated FSH levels.

 

Hormones of Spermatogenesis:

Follicular stimulating hormone:

  • FSH is essential for the initial development of spermatogonia cells.
  • Main targets of FSH action include:
    • Proliferation of Sertoli cell
    • Proliferation of Spermatogonia up to primary spermatocyte stage
    • Support the process of meiosis.

Testosterone:

  • Testosterone is particularly required for the terminal stages of spermatogenesis
  • Main targets of testosterone action include:
    • Spermiogenesis (spermatid to mature sperm)
    • Spermiation (release of sperm)
    • Meiosis (suppression of testosterone leads to block in meiosis)

Estrogen:

  • Main targets of Estrogen include:
    • Fluid resorption and concentration of sperm
    • Acrosome biogenesis of sperm

Growth hormone:

  • Growth hormone specifically promotes early division of the spermatogonia

 

Option A) Secretion of testosterone in response to LH stimulation is a function of Leydig cell

Option B) Production of inhibin leading to increased FSH levels simply does not explain the low testosterone levels seen in this patient

Option C) While testosterone does play a role in spermatogenesis, its production is mainly stimulated by LH acting on Leydig cells.

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old male with a history of aortic stenosis, hypertension, and recent cerebral venous thrombosis on anticoagulant therapy is scheduled for lower limb surgery. The anesthesiology team is evaluating the use of spinal anaesthesia. Which of the following is not a contraindication for spinal anaesthesia in this patient?
questions.solution: > is not a contraindication for spinal anaesthesia. Spinal anaesthesia can be safely used in patients with well-controlled hypertension. It is essential to monitor blood pressure closely during and after the procedure, as spinal anaesthesia can cause hypotension due to sympathetic blockade. Contraindications of Spinal Anesthesia Absolute Contraindications Patient refusal Localized sepsis Allergy to planned medications Patient's inability to remain still Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) Relative Contraindications Myelopathy or Peripheral Neuropathy Spinal Stenosis Previous spine surgery Neural Tube Defects Inherited Coagulopathy System infections Cardiac valvular stenosis Multiple sclerosis Anticoagulant medication Aortic stenosis ( Option A) decreases the heart’s ability to maintain adequate blood flow. The sudden drop in blood pressure from spinal anaesthesia could lead to dangerously low coronary perfusion and cardiac ischemia. Cerebral venous thrombosis (Option B), combined with anticoagulant therapy, is a contraindication for spinal anaesthesia due to the risk of elevated intracranial pressure and bleeding complications. Vertebral osteomyelitis (Option C): Introducing a needle into an infected area carries a high risk of spreading the infection to the spinal canal, potentially leading to meningitis or epidural abscess. @Neet_pg_bot

The patient reports similar episodes resolving within 10-14 days. What is the most common cause of this condition?
questions.solution: g> acute sinusitis, most commonly caused by a viral infection from upper respiratory viruses like rhinovirus, influenza, or parainfluenza. Allergic fungal sinusitis (Option B) is typically associated with chronic sinusitis, not acute episodes, and is more common in patients with atopy or asthma. Chronic Sinusitis is defined as inflammation of the sinuses and nasal passages lasting more than 12 weeks despite medical treatment. It is characterised by symptoms such as nasal obstruction, facial pain or pressure, nasal discharge, and a reduction in the sense of smell. Causes of Chronic Sinusitis Category Contributing Factors Patient Factors Anatomic structural deformities : Obstruction of sinus ostia (e.g., deviated septum, concha bullosa, anatomical variations) (Option A) Lifestyle factors : Smoking, snuff dipping, prolonged use of intranasal medications Immune Deficiency Primary : IgG deficiency, primary ciliary dyskinesia, cystic fibrosis Acquired : HIV, prolonged steroid use, chemotherapy, immunosuppressants in organ transplant patients, leukaemia Aspirin Sensitivity Sensitivity to aspirin causing chronic airway inflammation. (Option D) Environmental Factors Aeroallergens : Allergic rhinitis, asthma, exposure to allergens (dust, pollen, moulds) Toxins and Chemicals : Exposure to pollution, occupational chemicals, and toxic gases. Pathogens Bacteria (aerobic and anaerobic), fungi, mycobacteria @Neet_pg_bot

g> acute sinusitis, most commonly caused by a viral infection from upper respiratory viruses like rhinovirus, influenza, or parainfluenza.

Allergic fungal sinusitis (Option B) is typically associated with chronic sinusitis, not acute episodes, and is more common in patients with atopy or asthma.

Chronic Sinusitis is defined as inflammation of the sinuses and nasal passages lasting more than 12 weeks despite medical treatment. It is characterised by symptoms such as nasal obstruction, facial pain or pressure, nasal discharge, and a reduction in the sense of smell.

 

Causes of Chronic Sinusitis

Category

Contributing Factors

Patient Factors

Anatomic structural deformities: Obstruction of sinus ostia (e.g., deviated septum, concha bullosa, anatomical variations) (Option A)

Lifestyle factors: Smoking, snuff dipping, prolonged use of intranasal medications

Immune Deficiency

Primary: IgG deficiency, primary ciliary dyskinesia, cystic fibrosis

Acquired: HIV, prolonged steroid use, chemotherapy, immunosuppressants in organ transplant patients, leukaemia

Aspirin Sensitivity

Sensitivity to aspirin causing chronic airway inflammation. (Option D)

Environmental Factors

Aeroallergens: Allergic rhinitis, asthma, exposure to allergens (dust, pollen, moulds)

Toxins and Chemicals: Exposure to pollution, occupational chemicals, and toxic gases.

Pathogens

Bacteria (aerobic and anaerobic), fungi, mycobacteria

options.text: Forms salt bridges with positively charged residues forming a relaxed structure

options.label: B
options.text: Disrupts salt bridges formed in the taut structure, decreasing oxygen affinity

options.label: C
options.text: Forms salt bridges with positively charged residues stabilising taut structure

options.label: D
options.text: Binds to the heme directly, decreasing the oxygen affinity

questions.answerText: Forms salt bridges with positively charged residues stabilising taut structure
questions.solution: Increased levels of 2,3-BPG stabilise the taut (T) structure of haemoglobin by forming salt bridges with positively charged residues. This stabilisation lowers haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, promoting oxygen release to tissues, which can be beneficial in conditions like anaemia. Effect of 2,3 BPG on Hb: Reduces the affinity of Hb for oxygen and helps unload oxygen to tissues. A by-product of glycolysis. (Rapaport Leubering Cycle) Mechanism: 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) binds with a pocket formed by the β chains in the deoxygenated state of hemoglobin. Forms salt bridges with positively charged residues forming a relaxed structure (Option A): Incorrect because salt bridges stabilize the T form , not the R form. Disrupts salt bridges formed in the taut structure, decreasing oxygen affinity (Option B): Incorrect because 2,3-BPG forms rather than disrupts salt bridges, stabilizing the T form. Binds to the heme directly, decreasing the oxygen affinity (Option D): Incorrect because 2,3-BPG does not bind to heme ; it binds between β-chains in deoxygenated Hb. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
• Increased levels of 2,3-BPG stabilise the taut (T) structure of haemoglobin by forming salt bridges with positively charged residues.
  • This stabilisation lowers haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, promoting oxygen release to tissues, which can be beneficial in conditions like anaemia.

Effect of 2,3 BPG on Hb:

  • Reduces the affinity of Hb for oxygen and helps unload oxygen to tissues.
  • A by-product of glycolysis. (Rapaport Leubering Cycle)

Mechanism:

2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) binds with a pocket formed by the β chains in the deoxygenated state of hemoglobin.

Forms salt bridges with positively charged residues forming a relaxed structure (Option A): Incorrect because salt bridges stabilize the T form, not the R form.

Disrupts salt bridges formed in the taut structure, decreasing oxygen affinity (Option B): Incorrect because 2,3-BPG forms rather than disrupts salt bridges, stabilizing the T form.

Binds to the heme directly, decreasing the oxygen affinity (Option D): Incorrect because 2,3-BPG does not bind to heme; it binds between β-chains in deoxygenated Hb.

questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old patient with diabetes presents with rapidly worsening vision. Upon examination, the ophthalmologist notes the presence of bilateral, snowflake-like white opacities in the cortex of the lens. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: an> cataract Explanation : Diabetic cataract ( also known as presenile cataract) is characterized by bilateral, snowflake-like white opacities in the lens cortex, typically seen in young adults with diabetes. Opacities may either resolve spontaneously or progress to maturity within days. Occurs due to sorbitol accumulation. Commonly seen in Type 1 diabetes. Senile cataract (Option A) typically affects older individuals, although it can occur earlier in diabetics; however, it does not present with snowflake-like opacities. Christmas tree cataract (Option B) is associated with myotonic dystrophy, not diabetes. Posterior subcapsular cataract (Option D) can be seen in various conditions, including myotonic dystrophy, but does not present with the snowflake-like opacity as seen in true diabetic cataract. @Neet_pg_bot

an> cataract

 

Explanation:

  • Diabetic cataract (also known as presenile cataract) is characterized by bilateral, snowflake-like white opacities in the lens cortex, typically seen in young adults with diabetes. Opacities may either resolve spontaneously or progress to maturity within days.

  • Commonly seen in Type 1 diabetes.

/strong>

The S(+) isomer of ketamine is more potent as an analgesic than the R(-) isomer.

Mechanisms of Action

  • Inhibits N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDA) receptors (Option A), affecting the CNS.
  • Induces dissociative anesthesia, making patients appear conscious but unable to process sensory input.
  • Influences endogenous analgesic pathways.
  • It is an analog of phencyclidine.
  • It is a racemic mixture of R(-) ketamine and S(+) ketamine.
  • Molecular weight: 238 kD
  • High lipid solubility (5 to 10 times that of thiopental) (Option C) and low protein binding (12%).
  • S(+) isomer (Ketanest) is 3 to 4 times more potent as an analgesic with fewer psychomimetic effects.
  • S(+) ketamine causes cognitive impairment and reduced reaction time despite its analgesic properties.
  • S(+) isomer has higher NMDA affinity and potency.

Pharmacokinetics

  • Absorption: Primarily given intravenously or intramuscularly; peak levels in 10-15 minutes.
  • Distribution: Highly lipid-soluble; rapid brain uptake with a 10-15 minute distribution half-life.
  • Biotransformation: Metabolized in the liver to active metabolites; tolerance develops with repeated use. (Option D)
  • Excretion: Renally excreted; elimination half-life of about 2 hours.

questions.stemHtml: A 34-year-old male presents with severe abdominal pain and inability to urinate after a car accident. On examination, he has diffuse abdominal tenderness with guarding and rigidity. A cystogram reveals urine leakage into the peritoneal cavity. What is the next best step in management?
questions.solution: rio, the patient presents with signs and symptoms of intraperitoneal bladder rupture, which is a surgical emergency. Therefore, emergency laparotomy is done immediately. Intraperitoneal rupture Involves a tear or injury to the peritoneum over the bladder, and urine leaks into the peritoneal cavity in males. Causes: Often occurs in a fully distended bladder, usually due to trauma or injury. Clinical Features: Sudden, severe pain in the suprapubic region. Signs of shock and syncope. Diffuse abdominal pain with later features of peritonitis. Abdominal distension. Haematuria Absence of desire to urinate. Diagnosis: Plain X-ray: May show ground glass appearance. Peritoneal Tap: Used to collect urine from the abdominal cavity. Cystography: Iodine dye is injected via a catheter to visualize bladder tears and the dye entry into the peritoneal cavity. The contrast outlines the bowel loops. Ultrasound: To assess other abdominal injuries. {{caption_text}} Treatment: Emergency Laparotomy is required. (Option B). Bladder tear is sutured with polylactic acid (vicryl) in two layers. Peritoneal wash to clean out the peritoneal cavity. Separate drainage for prevesical space and peritoneal cavity. Administration of specific antibiotics to prevent sepsis. Catheterization: Malecot’s catheter is placed suprapubically. Foley's catheter passed urethrally. Complications: Cystitis /and pyelonephritis. Peritonitis. Pelvic abscess. Fistula formation (vesicovaginal or rectovesical). Paralytic ileus. Hemorrhage. Prognosis: 100% mortality without surgery. @Neet_pg_bot

Pathogenesis of Thyroid Eye Disease (Graves' Orbitopathy) Thyroid eye disease (TED) is an autoimmune inflammatory disorder associated with Graves’ disease. Primary autoimmune target: orbital fibroblasts → these fibroblasts differentiate into adipocytes and myofibroblasts under the effect of T-cell–mediated cytokines. This leads to: Pleomorphic inflammatory infiltration Increased secretion of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) Water retention Enlargement of orbital fat and extraocular muscles These changes raise intraorbital pressure → producing the hallmark features of TED: Proptosis Restricted ocular motility (restrictive myopathy, esp. inferior rectus fibrosis → impaired elevation) Optic neuropathy Lid retraction and lid lag Soft tissue congestion Extraocular muscles are affected secondarily (Option A). The autoimmune attack is primarily directed at orbital fibroblasts, not the muscles themselves. The earliest defective ocular movement is elevation (Option B) due to inferior rectus fibrosis (restrictive myopathy). Infiltration is pleomorphic (mixed inflammatory cells), not predominantly neutrophils (Option D). @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ustomMeta" data-dictid="799202e6fe16927772009a1501b0a8">thyroid eye disease (Graves’ orbitopathy), where T-cells attack orbital fibroblasts and adipocytes.

Pathogenesis of Thyroid Eye Disease (Graves' Orbitopathy)

  • Thyroid eye disease (TED) is an autoimmune inflammatory disorder associated with Graves’ disease.
  • Primary autoimmune target: orbital fibroblasts → these fibroblasts differentiate into adipocytes and myofibroblasts under the effect of T-cell–mediated cytokines.
  • This leads to:
    • Pleomorphic inflammatory infiltration
    • Increased secretion of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs)
    • Water retention
    • Enlargement of orbital fat and extraocular muscles
  • These changes raise intraorbital pressure → producing the hallmark features of TED:
    • Proptosis
    • Restricted ocular motility (restrictive myopathy, esp. inferior rectus fibrosis → impaired elevation)
    • Optic neuropathy
    • Lid retraction and lid lag
    • Soft tissue congestion

 

Extraocular muscles are affected secondarily (Option A). The autoimmune attack is primarily directed at orbital fibroblasts, not the muscles themselves.
 

The earliest defective ocular movement is elevation (Option B) due to inferior rectus fibrosis (restrictive myopathy).
 

Infiltration is pleomorphic (mixed inflammatory cells), not predominantly neutrophils (Option D).

options.label: A
options.text: It can occur in association with hypospadias.

options.label: B
options.text: The most common site of arrest of descent is the inguinal canal.

options.label: C
options.text: It is very commonly associated with a well-defined hormonal disorder.

questions.answerText: It is very commonly associated with a well-defined hormonal disorder.
questions.solution: f the intra-abdominal testes to descend into the scrotal sac, associated with testicular dysfunction and an increased risk of testicular cancer. It usually occurs as an isolated anomaly but may be accompanied by other genitourinary tract malformations, such as hypospadias. (Option A) The normal descent of the testes occurs in two phases: Transabdominal phase: Mediated by Mullerian inhibiting substance. Inguinoscrotal phase: Mediated by the androgen-induced release of calcitonin-related gene peptide. Any problem in any of these descents can lead to cryptorchidism. Sites of arrest of descent: Inguinal canal (most common). (Option B) Abdomen (uncommon). When the testis fails to descend into the scrotum, it is deprived of the temperature needed for spermatogenesis. As a result, sperm production does not occur, and the seminiferous tubules contain only Sertoli cells ( Sertoli cell–only syndrome ). Leydig cells outside the tubules may appear prominent—not from true hypertrophy or hyperplasia, but due to the absence of germ cells—though this prominence is often mistakenly reported as Leydig cell hyperplasia . (Option D) @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A middle-aged woman presents with a history of recurrent painful, pustular lesions on scalp which heals with scarring. She is healthy otherwise with no history of similar lesions. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
questions.stemHtml: A middle-aged woman presents with a history of recurrent painful, pustular lesions on scalp which heals with scarring. She is healthy otherwise with no history of similar lesions. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?

options.label: A
options.text: The culture of extracted hair alone.

options.label: B
options.text: Culture of extracted hair with patient-collected hair sheddings.

options.label: C
options.text: Shave biopsy of scalp and culture of extracted hair.

options.label: D
options.text: Punch biopsy of scalp and culture of extracted hair.

questions.answerText: Punch biopsy of scalp and culture of extracted hair.
questions.solution: Explanation: The patient presented with a history of recurrent painful, pustular lesions on the scalp which heal with scarring suggests the diagnosis of Folliculitis decalvans . A punch biopsy of the scalp and culture of extracted hair is the most appropriate investigation. Folliculitis decalvans: Folliculitis decalvans or tufted hair folliculitis is a progressive pattern of cicatricial alopecia of the scalp. Its characteristic feature is the presence of multiple tufts of hair emerging from a single follicular opening also known as Doll’s hair appearance The images below depict the scaring alopecia seen in Folliculitis decalvans. Diagnosis is based on clinical and histological findings. Ideal biopsy tissue should contain clinical signs of scarring, no follicular ostia, and active inflammation (pustules, erythema, etc.). Hence, a punch biopsy that extends into the subcutaneous fat is our preferred procedure for the pathologic evaluation of FD. Oral antibiotics (Tetracyclines) are the mainstay treatment. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

The patient presented with a history of recurrent painful, pustular lesions on the scalp which heal with scarring suggests the diagnosis of Folliculitis decalvans. A punch biopsy of the scalp and culture of extracted hair is the most appropriate investigation.

Folliculitis decalvans:

  • Folliculitis decalvans or tufted hair folliculitis is a progressive pattern of cicatricial alopecia of the scalp.
  • Its characteristic feature is the presence of multiple tufts of hair emerging from a single follicular opening also known as Doll’s hair appearance
  • The images below depict the scaring alopecia seen in Folliculitis decalvans.

 

  • Diagnosis is based on clinical and histological findings. Ideal biopsy tissue should contain clinical signs of scarring, no follicular ostia, and active inflammation (pustules, erythema, etc.).
  • Hence, a punch biopsy that extends into the subcutaneous fat is our preferred procedure for the pathologic evaluation of FD.
  • Oral antibiotics (Tetracyclines) are the mainstay treatment.

questions.solution: Correct Answer: D) Non-ionic Monomer Iohexol is an iodine contrast agent that is classified as a Non-ionic monomer . The commonly used iodine contrast agents are water soluble and are classified into ionic and non-ionic groups based on their osmolality and chemical structure. The iodine particle ratio helps decide the osmolality of the drug, where high osmolar drugs pose a higher risk for kidney damage. Iodine Particle Ratio Ionic = 2 particles Non-ionic = 1 particle Monomer = 3 iodine Dimer = 6 iodine Ionic Monomer Ionic Dimer Non-ionic Monomer Non-ionic Dimer 3:2 (High osmolality) 3:1 (Low osmolality) 3:1 6:1 Iodine Contrast Routes of administration Intravenous and Intra-arterial Indications Commonly used for contrast in CECT (3D X-ray), Interventional Radiology, and X-rays like as in Intravenous pyelogram Micturating cystourethrogram Hysterosalpingography Retrograde pyelography ERCP- Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography Adverse Reactions Physiological Reactions Allergic Reactions Post-contrast induced nephropathy Nausea Vomiting Flushing Headaches Vasovagal reaction Arrhythmias Seizures - Mild reactions: Hives (Urticaria) Erythema (Redness of skin) Moderate to severe reactions: Wheezing Anaphylactoid reactions (Non-IgE mediated) Also known as Contrast-Induced Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) . It is defined as an increase in serum creatinine by > 0.5 mg/dL or a > 25% rise from the baseline within 3 days of contrast administration, without any other clear cause. in infarction is associated with delayed deaths rather than early deaths by hanging.
