Death in Hanging

The usual period for death is 3–5 minutes and this can extend to 5–8 minutes of suspension leading to death.

  1. Immediate Death:
    • Occurs if cervical vertebrae are fractured.
    • This can happen if there is inhibition of the heart.
  2. Rapid Death:
    • Usually results from asphyxia.
  3. Least Rapid Death:
    • If coma is the cause, death occurs more slowly.


 

Causes of Death from Hanging

  1. Asphyxia: The constricting force of the ligature compresses the larynx and trachea, leading to asphyxia. (Option A ruled out)
  2. Venous Congestion: If the ligature is broad and soft, it can block the jugular veins, halting cerebral circulation. (Option C ruled out)
  3. Combined Asphyxia and Venous Congestion: This is the most common cause of death in hanging cases.
  4. Cerebral Anemia: Occurs when a thin cord is used as a ligature, reducing blood flow to the brain.
  5. Reflex Vagal Inhibition: This can result in sudden cardiac arrest. (Option D ruled out)
  6. Fracture/Dislocation of Cervical Vertebrae: Commonly seen in judicial hangings.

 

Delayed Deaths

Rarely, delayed deaths may result from:

  • Aspiration pneumonia
  • Edema of the lungs or larynx
  • Infections
  • Brain infarction (Option B)
  • Hypoxic encephalopathy
  • Brain abscess

questions.stem: A 60-year-old patient is scheduled for an MRI to evaluate cognitive changes. Which of the following systems is specifically designed to provide shielding against radio frequency interference during the scan?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old patient is scheduled for an MRI to evaluate cognitive changes. Which of the following systems is specifically designed to provide shielding against radio frequency interference during the scan?
questions.solution: A Faraday cage is a conductive enclosure that shields its inner space from electromagnetic interference. In MRI environments, this enclosure is typically constructed using wooden panels wrapped in copper wires, which provide effective radiofrequency (RF) shielding. This shielding helps minimize interference, which leads to imaging artifacts and ensures clearer and more accurate MRI results. In the MRI facility, the cage is often visible through the special window glass separating the control room from the scanner area, further emphasizing its role in maintaining optimal imaging conditions. Gradient Coils (Option A) are three sets, X, Y, and Z, used in the MRI imaging process to create intentional variations in the main magnetic field. These changes in the magnetic field enable the localisation of image slices. Helmholtz coils (Option B) are a pair of circular coils arranged parallel to one another and function as Z gradient coils in MRI scanners. Shim coils (Option C) are used to correct minor spatial discrepancies in the main static magnetic field and ensure optimal spatial uniformity, improving MRI image quality by reducing artifacts. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Explanation: The POCSO Act is gender-neutral, and it protects all children, not just female children, under the age of 18 from sexual abuse. Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act Enacted in 2012, it is law in India designed to protect children under the age of 18 from sexual abuse, sexual harassment, and pornography. Key Features of the POCSO Act: Gender-neutral law (Option A) It covers penetrative and non-penetrative assault, sexual harassment, and use of children for pornography Burden of proof is on the accused, unlike many other criminal laws where the burden is on the prosecution Mandatory reporting by adults and failure to do so can be punishable Special courts for the trial of offenses to ensure a child-friendly environment Identity of the victim is to be protected, and the proceedings are to be conducted in camera to prevent exposure Recent Changes and Developments in the POCSO Act: 2019 Amendment (Option C ruled out) Stricter Punishments: Death penalty for aggravated sexual assault against children The minimum punishment for penetrative sexual assault increased to 10 years, and for aggravated penetrative sexual assault increased to 20 years, with the possibility of life imprisonment or death in extreme cases. Fast-track Courts to ensure swift disposal of POCSO cases, given the backlog of pending cases. (Option D ruled out) Clarifications on ‘Touch’ and Sexual Intent: The intent behind physical contact is crucial in determining whether it qualifies as an offense under POCSO. questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation: The POCSO Act is gender-neutral, and it protects all children, not just female children, under the age of 18 from sexual abuse.

 

Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act

Enacted in 2012, it is law in India designed to protect children under the age of 18 from sexual abuse, sexual harassment, and pornography.

 

Key Features of the POCSO Act:

  • Gender-neutral law (Option A)
  • It covers penetrative and non-penetrative assault, sexual harassment, and use of children for pornography
  • Burden of proof is on the accused, unlike many other criminal laws where the burden is on the prosecution
  • Mandatory reporting by adults and failure to do so can be punishable
  • Special courts for the trial of offenses to ensure a child-friendly environment
  • Identity of the victim is to be protected, and the proceedings are to be conducted in camera to prevent exposure

 

Recent Changes and Developments in the POCSO Act:

  • 2019 Amendment (Option C ruled out)
    • Stricter Punishments: Death penalty for aggravated sexual assault against children
    • The minimum punishment for penetrative sexual assault increased to 10 years, and for aggravated penetrative sexual assault increased to 20 years, with the possibility of life imprisonment or death in extreme cases.
  • Fast-track Courts to ensure swift disposal of POCSO cases, given the backlog of pending cases. (Option D ruled out)
  • Clarifications on ‘Touch’ and Sexual Intent:
    • The intent behind physical contact is crucial in determining whether it qualifies as an offense under POCSO.
  • Digital Crimes Against Children: (Option B ruled out)
    • Provisions related to the use of children for pornographic and online exploitation purposes have been emphasized with stricter penalties.

questions.stemHtml: Which health management technique is used for creating a graphical representation of all events and activities required to complete a project enabling timely project completion?
questions.solution: ong> Programme Evaluation and Review Technique (PERT) is a type of quantitative health management method that involves creating a graphical representation (often an Arrow Diagram) of all events and activities required to complete a project. Notify the surgeon and call for assistance. Hyperventilate the patient with 100% oxygen at a fresh flow rate of at least 10 L/min. questions.solutionHtml:
rity in managing malignant hyperthermia is to immediately discontinue the triggering agents—halothane and succinylcholine—and then hyperventilate the patient with 100% oxygen. This helps to counteract hypoxia and stabilize the patient's condition.

 

Diagnosis of malignant hyperthermia

  • Best screening test- Creatine kinase test
  • Gold Standard Diagnostic test- Halothane-Caffeine Test

 

Treatment for malignant hyperthermia

  1. Discontinue volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine immediately. Notify the surgeon and call for assistance.
  2. Hyperventilate the patient with 100% oxygen at a fresh flow rate of at least 10 L/min.
  3. Mix dantrolene sodium with sterile distilled water and administer 2.5 mg/kg intravenously as soon as possible. Repeat every 5 to 10 minutes until symptoms improve, with a maximum total dose of 10 mg/kg.
  4. Administer bicarbonate to address metabolic acidosis.
  5. Implement cooling measures, such as lavage, cooling blankets, and cold intravenous fluids.
  6. For severe hyperkalemia, administer dextrose (25–50 g IV) along with regular insulin (10–20 units IV for adults).
  7. Provide antiarrhythmic medications as necessary.
  8. Monitor end-tidal CO2 levels, electrolytes, blood gases, creatine kinase, serum myoglobin, core temperature, urinary output and colour, and coagulation status.

 

Administer dantrolene and bicarbonate immediately. (Option A): While dantrolene is critical, it should not be the first action. Stopping the triggers and ensuring oxygenation takes priority.

Administer dantrolene and continue the surgery with halothane only. (Option C): Continuing halothane use after administering dantrolene can worsen the condition.

Administer cold IV fluids with dantrolene. (Option D): While cold IV fluids and dantrolene are important for treatment, they should not be the first actions. Stopping the anesthetics and providing oxygen must come first for immediate stabilization.

questions.stem: Which structure, located in the petrous part of the temporal bone, is responsible for transmitting the facial nerve (VII) and is commonly involved in pathological conditions such as acoustic neuroma affecting the cerebellopontine angle?
questions.stemHtml: Which structure, located in the petrous part of the temporal bone, is responsible for transmitting the facial nerve (VII) and is commonly involved in pathological conditions such as acoustic neuroma affecting the cerebellopontine angle?
questions.solution: >internal auditory canal, located in the petrous part of the temporal bone, transmits both the facial nerve (VII) and the vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII). Pathological conditions like acoustic neuroma, which arises from the vestibular division of the vestibulocochlear nerve, commonly affect this canal and extend into the cerebellopontine angle, leading to symptoms involving both hearing and facial nerve function. Anatomy of the Temporal Bone Segments 1. Tympanic : Forms the external auditory canal (EAC). 2. Mastoid: Contains the mastoid air cell system, which is essential for ventilation and drainage of the middle ear. Includes the antrum, connected to the epitympanum, and surrounded by air cells. 3. Petrous : Most medial part, containing the cochlea, vestibule, semicircular canals and internal auditory canal. Houses the facial nerve (VII) and vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII). 4. questions.solution: ecule of muscle glycogen undergoes anaerobic glycolysis (glycogen → lactate), the net ATP yield differs from glucose metabolism because glycogen breakdown bypasses the hexokinase step , which normally consumes ATP. Here’s a stepwise explanation: Glycogenolysis (Breakdown of Glycogen) Glycogen phosphorylase removes glucose units from glycogen as glucose-1-phosphate (G1P) . Phosphoglucomutase converts G1P to glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) . Since G6P is directly obtained, it skips the hexokinase step (which normally consumes 1 ATP in glucose metabolism). Glycolysis (Conversion of Glucose-6-Phosphate to Pyruvate) G6P enters glycolysis and follows the usual pathway. Key ATP-related steps: Energy investment: 1 ATP is used at the phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) step. Energy generation: 4 ATP are produced from substrate-level phosphorylation . Net ATP gain from glycolysis: 4 ATP (produced) - 1 ATP (used) = 3 ATP . Anaerobic Conditions (Conversion of Pyruvate to Lactate) In anaerobic exercise (e.g., intense training), pyruvate is converted to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) . This step does not produce or consume ATP ; its main role is regenerating NAD⁺ for continued glycolysis. ATP Yield Calculation from Muscle Glycogen Breakdown Step Process ATP Change Glycogenolysis Glycogen → Glucose-1-phosphate → Glucose-6-phosphate (no ATP used) +0 ATP Glycolysis Glucose-6-phosphate → 2 Pyruvate +4 ATP Energy Consumption ATP used in glycolysis (Phosphofructokinase-1 step) -1 ATP Anaerobic Conversion 2 Pyruvate → 2 Lactate (No ATP change) 0 ATP Net ATP Yield 3 ATP Final Net ATP Yield: Glycolysis from muscle glycogen produces 3 ATP (instead of 2 ATP when starting from free glucose) because the hexokinase step is bypassed. No additional ATP is lost or gained during lactate formation. Total ATP yield per glycogen molecule → 3 ATP. 1 ATP (Option A): Incorrect because the actual ATP yield is higher . Even free glucose metabolism yields 2 ATP , and muscle glycogen yields 3 ATP due to bypassing hexokinase. 2 ATP (Option B): Incorrect because this is the ATP yield when glucose (not glycogen) is used . Muscle glycogen metabolism produces one extra ATP by skipping the ATP-consuming hexokinase step. 4 ATP (Option D): Incorrect because glycolysis does produce 4 ATP, but 1 ATP is consumed at the PFK-1 step , leading to a net gain of 3 ATP, not 4 . @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ecule of muscle glycogen undergoes anaerobic glycolysis (glycogen → lactate), the net ATP yield differs from glucose metabolism because glycogen breakdown bypasses the hexokinase step, which normally consumes ATP. Here’s a stepwise explanation:

  1. Glycogenolysis (Breakdown of Glycogen)

    • Glycogen phosphorylase removes glucose units from glycogen as glucose-1-phosphate (G1P).
    • Phosphoglucomutase converts G1P to glucose-6-phosphate (G6P).
    • Since G6P is directly obtained, it skips the hexokinase step (which normally consumes 1 ATP in glucose metabolism).

  2. Glycolysis (Conversion of Glucose-6-Phosphate to Pyruvate)

    • G6P enters glycolysis and follows the usual pathway.
    • Key ATP-related steps:
      • Energy investment: 1 ATP is used at the phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) step.
      • Energy generation: 4 ATP are produced from substrate-level phosphorylation.
      • Net ATP gain from glycolysis: 4 ATP (produced) - 1 ATP (used) = 3 ATP.

  3. Anaerobic Conditions (Conversion of Pyruvate to Lactate)

    • In anaerobic exercise (e.g., intense training), pyruvate is converted to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH).
    • This step does not produce or consume ATP; its main role is regenerating NAD⁺ for continued glycolysis.

ATP Yield Calculation from Muscle Glycogen Breakdown

Step Process ATP Change
Glycogenolysis Glycogen → Glucose-1-phosphate → Glucose-6-phosphate (no ATP used) +0 ATP
Glycolysis Glucose-6-phosphate → 2 Pyruvate +4 ATP
Energy Consumption ATP used in glycolysis (Phosphofructokinase-1 step) -1 ATP
Anaerobic Conversion 2 Pyruvate → 2 Lactate (No ATP change) 0 ATP
Net ATP Yield   3 ATP

Final Net ATP Yield:

  • Glycolysis from muscle glycogen produces 3 ATP (instead of 2 ATP when starting from free glucose) because the hexokinase step is bypassed.
  • No additional ATP is lost or gained during lactate formation.
  • Total ATP yield per glycogen molecule → 3 ATP.

1 ATP (Option A):

  • Incorrect because the actual ATP yield is higher. Even free glucose metabolism yields 2 ATP, and muscle glycogen yields 3 ATP due to bypassing hexokinase.

2 ATP (Option B):

  • Incorrect because this is the ATP yield when glucose (not glycogen) is used. Muscle glycogen metabolism produces one extra ATP by skipping the ATP-consuming hexokinase step.

4 ATP (Option D):

  • Incorrect because glycolysis does produce 4 ATP, but 1 ATP is consumed at the PFK-1 step, leading to a net gain of 3 ATP, not 4.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with galactorrhea (inappropriate milk secretion) and menstrual irregularities. After excluding other causes, the physician considers a potential pituitary dysfunction. Which hypothalamic hormone contributes to increased prolactin levels in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman presents with galactorrhea (inappropriate milk secretion) and menstrual irregularities. After excluding other causes, the physician considers a potential pituitary dysfunction. Which hypothalamic hormone contributes to increased prolactin levels in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct answer: C) Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) , in addition to its primary role in stimulating TSH release from the anterior pituitary, can also increase prolactin secretion. This dual effect may contribute to conditions like galactorrhea when prolactin levels are elevated. The pituitary gland plays a pivotal role in regulating various endocrine functions, including growth, metabolism, and reproduction. The activity of the pituitary gland is primarily governed by the hypothalamus , which releases specific hormones, either stimulating or inhibiting, that reach the pituitary. The regulation of pituitary hormone secretion is a finely tuned process, primarily controlled by feedback mechanisms. Negative feedback loops are the most common, where the end products of a hormone's action inhibit further hormone release to maintain homeostasis. An example is cortisol, which inhibits its own secretion through feedback on both the hypothalamus and pituitary. Positive feedback, although less common, occurs in processes like childbirth, where oxytocin release enhances uterine contractions, leading to further oxytocin release. A) Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) : This hormone primarily stimulates the release of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) from the anterior pituitary, which in turn influences cortisol production by the adrenal glands. CRH does not directly affect prolactin levels. B) Dopamine : This neurotransmitter serves as the primary inhibitor of prolactin secretion. Increased dopamine levels typically decrease prolactin release, the opposite of what is described in the scenario. D) Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) : This hormone primarily regulates the release of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which are involved in reproductive function. GnRH does not significantly influence prolactin secretion. @Neet_pg_bot

    • Positive feedback, although less common, occurs in processes like childbirth, where oxytocin release enhances uterine contractions, leading to further oxytocin release.

A) Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH): This hormone primarily stimulates the release of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) from the anterior pituitary, which in turn influences cortisol production by the adrenal glands. CRH does not directly affect prolactin levels.

 

B) Dopamine: This neurotransmitter serves as the primary inhibitor of prolactin secretion. Increased dopamine levels typically decrease prolactin release, the opposite of what is described in the scenario.

 

D) Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH): This hormone primarily regulates the release of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which are involved in reproductive function. GnRH does not significantly influence prolactin secretion.

questions.stemHtml:
A 29-year-old woman presents with complaints of infertility and chronic lower abdominal pain for the past year. She mentions recent unintentional weight loss and occasional night sweats. Her menstrual cycles have been regular, but she has experienced heavier-than-usual periods over the past six months. Considering her symptoms and clinical history, the clinician suspects endometrial tuberculosis and decides to perform an endometrial biopsy for diagnosis.
Which is the best time to perform an endometrial biopsy to diagnose endometrial tuberculosis?

options.label: D
options.text: Any time during the menstrual cycle

questions.solution: The optimal time to perform an endometrial biopsy for diagnosing endometrial tuberculosis is during the late premenstrual phase of the menstrual cycle. The tubercle is found in the basal layer of the endometrium and moves to the surface before menstruation. Following the shedding of the endometrium during menstruation, reinfection arises from the basal layer lesions or the fallopian tubes. Layers affected: Endometrial tuberculosis typically affects the endometrial layer (60%) while sparing the myometrium. Endometrial biopsy is done during the premenstrual period by D&C or hysteroscopy directed biopsy. Menstrual blood collected on the first day of menstruation (superficial layer is shed off) can also be used as a diagnostic sample because it may contain the bacilli responsible for the infection. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: trong> The given clinical condition is diagnosed as Acne vulgaris, a chronic inflammatory skin condition associated with increased sebum production and the accumulation of dead skin cells within the follicles. Comedones are clogged hair follicles (pores) that contain a mixture of oil (sebum) and dead skin cells. They are the hallmark lesions of acne vulgaris. They are non-inflammatory lesions and are of two types: Open comedones (blackheads): These are follicles with a wider opening to the skin's surface and are not covered by the epidermis. When exposed to air, the keratin plug becomes oxidized and appears black. Closed comedones (whiteheads): These are follicles with a narrower opening to the skin's surface and are covered by the epidermis. The accumulation of sebum and dead skin cells creates a white or flesh-coloured bump beneath the skin's surface. It primarily affects individuals over the age of 40 and is also seen in adolescents (Option A): Acne vulgaris is typically seen in puberty and adolescence, not above the age of 40 years. It is not influenced by hormonal factors (Option B): Hormonal fluctuations, particularly increased levels of androgens (such as testosterone), can stimulate sebaceous gland activity, leading to increased sebum production. They are often associated with hormonal conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH). Genetic predisposition is not a contributing factor (Option D) : Genetic factors influence various aspects of acne development, including sebum production, follicular hyperkeratinization, and inflammatory responses. Thus, Genetic predisposition is a contributing factor to the development of acne vulgaris. @Neet_pg_bot

Open comedones (blackheads): These are follicles with a wider opening to the skin's surface and are not covered by the epidermis. When exposed to air, the keratin plug becomes oxidized and appears black.

Closed comedones (whiteheads): These are follicles with a narrower opening to the skin's surface and are covered by the epidermis. The accumulation of sebum and dead skin cells creates a white or flesh-coloured bump beneath the skin's surface.

It primarily affects individuals over the age of 40 and is also seen in adolescents (Option A): Acne vulgaris is typically seen in puberty and adolescence, not above the age of 40 years.

It is not influenced by hormonal factors (Option B): Hormonal fluctuations, particularly increased levels of androgens (such as testosterone), can stimulate sebaceous gland activity, leading to increased sebum production. They are often associated with hormonal conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH).

Genetic predisposition is not a contributing factor (Option D) : Genetic factors influence various aspects of acne development, including sebum production, follicular hyperkeratinization, and inflammatory responses. Thus, Genetic predisposition is a contributing factor to the development of acne vulgaris.

ith halothane-induced hepatitis, also known as Type-2 halothane hepatotoxicity. This is an immune-mediated reaction that typically occurs 1-2 weeks after exposure to halothane, especially in patients with previous exposure or risk factors such as moderate alcohol use.

Halothane

Category

Details

Chemical Properties

- Clear, heavy, colorless liquid

- Sweet, non-irritating odor, photosensitive (stored in an amber bottle with thymol preservative)

- Structure of an alkane

- Highly soluble in blood and tissues, hence can cause delayed recovery

Systemic Effects

- Cardiovascular: Myocardial depression, sensitization to catecholamines

- Respiratory: Respiratory depression

- Central Nervous System: General anesthesia, increased cerebral blood flow

Uses

- Induction and maintenance of general anesthesia

- Less commonly used now due to side effect profile

- Still used in some resource-limited settings

Side Effects

- Type 1 Hepatotoxicity: Mild, self-limiting liver injury (20-30% of patients)

- Type 2 Hepatotoxicity (Halothane Hepatitis): Severe, potentially fatal (1 in 35,000 after single exposure)

- Cardiorespiratory instability

- Arrhythmias, especially in children

- Malignant hyperthermia (rare)

Metabolism

- 20-45% metabolized in the liver

- Produces trifluoroacetyl (TFA) protein adducts which are immunogenic and are responsible for causing halothane hepatitis.

questions.stemHtml: A 48-year-old woman with a 10-year history of poorly controlled hypertension visits your clinic for follow-up. Her blood pressure is 158/96 mmHg, despite being on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide. Her serum creatinine and potassium levels are within normal limits. Which calcium channel blockers would be the most appropriate addition to her long-term blood pressure control treatment regimen?
questions.solution: Amlodipine is a long-acting dihydropyridine CCB, and it would be an appropriate choice to achieve better blood pressure control in the long term. It can be used as an add-on therapy with other antihypertensive agents, and its once-daily dosing improves patient compliance. Mechanism of action of CCB (Dihydropyridines): It blocks the entry of calcium ions through the L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle cells, causing vasodilation and a reduction in peripheral vascular resistance. Drug Use Rationale for Choice Nifedipine (Option A) Short-acting Primarily used for angina pectoris Not recommended for long-term hypertension management due to its short duration of action and potential for reflex tachycardia. Nicardipine (Option B) Short-acting Commonly used in the management of hypertensive emergencies and perioperative hypertension or severe hypertension in the intensive care unit. The short duration of action makes it less suitable for long-term hypertension management. Clevidipine (Option C) Ultra-short-acting Very short half-life makes it unsuitable for long-term hypertension management. Amlodipine (Option D) Long-acting. Recommended as a first-line or add-on therapy for the long-term management of hypertension Preferred choice due to its long duration of action (up to 24 hours), once-daily dosing, and effectiveness in lowering blood pressure with good tolerability. @Neet_pg_bot

Transmission of YF:

  • Vector: Aedes aegypti (tiger mosquito).

    • Rarely, encephalitis.

  • Vaccine – Live attenuated, 17-D strain

  • India not endemic – given free at airports/seaports for travelers

  • Not given in immunocompromised & egg allergy

  • Certificate issued on day 10

  • Validity: Lifetime

In contrast, Anopheles mosquitoes primarily transmit Malaria and are not involved in yellow fever transmission. The specific clinical features, such as hemorrhagic manifestations and liver necrosis, confirm the role of Aedes aegypti as the vector for this disease.

Culex (Option C): The clinical features suggest yellow fever, which is transmitted by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, not Culex. Culex primarily transmits diseases like Japanese encephalitis and West Nile virus. Additionally, Aedes aegypti feeds during the day and breeds in clean, standing water found in artificial containers, whereas Culex mosquitoes are more nocturnal and prefer polluted, stagnant water.

Mansonia (Option D): The clinical features indicate yellow fever, transmitted by Aedes aegypti, not Mansonia. Aedes aegypti is specifically known for yellow fever transmission, while Mansonia primarily transmits filarial infections. Thus, Aedes aegypti is the vector responsible for yellow fever.

Which of the following best describes the physiological consequence of this mutation?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman presents with signs of progressive muscle weakness and fatigue. She is diagnosed with a rare genetic disorder affecting intercellular communication in her skeletal and cardiac muscles. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in a connexin protein. Which of the following best describes the physiological consequence of this mutation?

options.label: A
options.text: Impaired electrical signal propagation between cardiac myocytes

options.label: D
options.text: Abnormal attachment of muscle fibers to the extracellular matrix

questions.answerText: Impaired electrical signal propagation between cardiac myocytes
questions.solution: id="e1fb96fd2416927771830dfed40e14">cardiac myocytes Explanation : Gap junctions, also called macula communicans, are specialized cell structures that facilitate direct communication between adjacent cells. They consist of channels formed by proteins called connexins, which allow ions, metabolites, and small molecules to pass between cells. Features of gap junctions: Connexons : Each channel is made of six connexin proteins that align between two cells to create a passage for substances like sodium, potassium, calcium, and small molecules. Electrical Communication : In tissues like cardiac and nerve cells, gap junctions enable rapid transmission of electrical impulses for synchronized function. Regulation : The channels can close in response to changes in pH or calcium levels, controlling the communication between cells. Distribution : Gap junctions are widely found in the body, playing a key role in lowering electrical resistance and supporting functions like electrical synapses in neurons Disruption of epithelial barrier function (Option B) : This is characteristic of defects in tight junctions (zonula occludens), which prevent paracellular leakage between epithelial cells. Tight junctions are unrelated to connexin proteins. Reduced mechanical stability between cells (Option C) : This describes the role of desmosomes , which provide structural integrity by linking intermediate filaments between cells. Desmosomes are crucial for mechanical stress resistance but have no role in direct cell communication. Abnormal attachment of muscle fibers to the extracellular matrix (Option D) : This refers to hemidesmosomes or integrins , which anchor cells to the basement membrane or extracellular matrix. These structures are involved in cell adhesion rather than communication through gap junctions. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
id="e1fb96fd2416927771830dfed40e14">cardiac myocytes

Explanation:

Gap junctions, also called macula communicans, are specialized cell structures that facilitate direct communication between adjacent cells. They consist of channels formed by proteins called connexins, which allow ions, metabolites, and small molecules to pass between cells.

 

Features of gap junctions:

  • Connexons: Each channel is made of six connexin proteins that align between two cells to create a passage for substances like sodium, potassium, calcium, and small molecules.
  • Electrical Communication: In tissues like cardiac and nerve cells, gap junctions enable rapid transmission of electrical impulses for synchronized function.
  • Regulation: The channels can close in response to changes in pH or calcium levels, controlling the communication between cells.

Distribution: Gap junctions are widely found in the body, playing a key role in lowering electrical resistance and supporting functions like electrical synapses in neurons

Disruption of epithelial barrier function (Option B): This is characteristic of defects in tight junctions (zonula occludens), which prevent paracellular leakage between epithelial cells. Tight junctions are unrelated to connexin proteins.


Reduced mechanical stability between cells (Option C): This describes the role of desmosomes, which provide structural integrity by linking intermediate filaments between cells. Desmosomes are crucial for mechanical stress resistance but have no role in direct cell communication.

 

Abnormal attachment of muscle fibers to the extracellular matrix (Option D): This refers to hemidesmosomes or integrins, which anchor cells to the basement membrane or extracellular matrix. These structures are involved in cell adhesion rather than communication through gap junctions.

questions.solution: ictid="7b1a7ff355169277719401475de6fb">ovary develops in the abdominal cavity from a genital ridge (formed from thickened coelomic epithelium) on the posterior abdominal wall, covering the mesonephros. It receives primordial germ cells from the yolk sac and then descends into the pelvis. During normal development, the descent is influenced by The gubernaculum (which later forms the round ligament of the ovary and the uterus ) and The processus vaginalis , an evagination of the peritoneum. In rare cases, the ovary may follow the round ligament and be drawn into the inguinal canal. This condition, known as imperfect descent of the ovary , can present clinically as a groin mass. It is not involved in guiding the descent of the ovary into the inguinal canal. questions.stem: A 28-year-old anxious female presents with hyperventilation during a panic attack. ABG shows: pH: 7.48 PaCO2: 20 mmHg HCO3-: 22 mEq/L Which acid-base disorder is present?
questions.stemHtml:
A 28-year-old anxious female presents with hyperventilation during a panic attack. ABG shows:
	pH: 7.48
	PaCO2: 20 mmHg
	HCO3-: 22 mEq/L
Which acid-base disorder is present?
questions.solution: customMeta" data-dictid="cfad80a0f716927771979aae100f95">respiratory alkalosis Explanation: In this case, the patient's panic attack has caused hyperventilation, leading to excessive CO2 washout (low PaCO2 of 30 mmHg, normal is 35-45 mmHg) The elevated pH of 7.48 (above normal 7.35-7.45) confirms alkalosis, while the low PaCO2 identifies it as respiratory in origin. We know that ACUTE : pH increases by 0.08 units and HCO3 decreases by 2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg decrease in PaCO2 CHRONIC : pH increases by 0.03 units and HCO3 decreases by 5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg decrease in PaCO2 In this patient ABG shows: pH: 7.48 PaCO2: 20 mmHg HCO3-: 20 mEq/L Normal PaCO2 - 38-42 mm hg Thus difference in PaCO2 = 42-22 = 20 mm hg As this patient is having an episode of anxiety attack, it is leading to acute respiratory alkalosis Thus pH should ↑ by 0.08 units and HCO3 ↓ by 2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↓ in PaCO2 pH should ↑ by 0.008 units and HCO3 ↓ by 0.2 mEq/L per 1 mmHg ↓ in PaCO2 For 20 mm hg fall in PaCO2 pH should ↑ by 0.16 units and HCO3 ↓ by 4 mEq/L (compensated) In this patient pH has ↑ 0.8 and HCO3 ↓ by 2 mEq/L (taking 7.40 as normal pH and 22-26 as normal serum HCO3- ) This pattern represents partial compensation because: 1) The pH remains elevated despite some compensation, 2) The HCO3- has started to decrease (compensation has begun), but 3) The compensation isn't enough to normalize the pH. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
customMeta" data-dictid="cfad80a0f716927771979aae100f95">respiratory alkalosis

Explanation:

  • In this case, the patient's panic attack has caused hyperventilation, leading to excessive CO2 washout (low PaCO2 of 30 mmHg, normal is 35-45 mmHg)
  • The elevated pH of 7.48 (above normal 7.35-7.45) confirms alkalosis, while the low PaCO2 identifies it as respiratory in origin.

We know that

  • ACUTE: pH increases by 0.08 units and HCO3 decreases by 2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg decrease in PaCO2
  • CHRONIC: pH increases by 0.03 units and HCO3 decreases by 5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg decrease in PaCO2
    • In this patient ABG shows:
  • pH: 7.48
  • PaCO2: 20 mmHg
  • HCO3-: 20 mEq/L
  • Normal PaCO2 - 38-42 mm hg

Thus difference in PaCO2 = 42-22 = 20 mm hg

 

As this patient is having an episode of anxiety attack, it is leading to acute respiratory alkalosis

  • Thus pH should ↑ by 0.08 units and HCO3 ↓ by 2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↓ in PaCO2
  • pH should ↑ by 0.008 units and HCO3 ↓ by 0.2 mEq/L per 1 mmHg ↓ in PaCO2
  • For 20 mm hg fall in PaCO2
    • pH should ↑ by 0.16 units and HCO3 ↓ by 4 mEq/L (compensated)
    • In this patient pH has ↑ 0.8 and HCO3 ↓ by 2 mEq/L (taking 7.40 as normal pH and 22-26 as normal serum HCO3- )

This pattern represents partial compensation because:

1) The pH remains elevated despite some compensation,

2) The HCO3- has started to decrease (compensation has begun), but

3) The compensation isn't enough to normalize the pH.

questions.solution: with fever, sore throat, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly is classic for infectious mononucleosis (IM) caused by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV). Diagnosis is supported by the Paul–Bunnell (Monospot) test , which detects heterophile IgM antibodies . These antibodies are non-specific and can agglutinate sheep or horse red blood cells —a hallmark of EBV infection. Examples of Heterophile Antigen Tests: Weil-Felix : Rickettsial infections Paul-Bunnell : Infectious mononucleosis Cold agglutination : Mycoplasma pneumonia Streptococcus MG : Streptococcal antibodies Paul-Bunnell Test Diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis caused by EBV. Utilizes sheep RBCs as antigens to detect heterophile antibodies in the patient’s serum. Principle : Heterophile antibodies agglutinate sheep RBCs; can occur rarely in normal individuals or after serum injections Procedure : Heat serum (56°C, 30 min), mix with 1% sheep RBCs in doubling dilutions, incubate 37°C for 4 hrs Interpretation : Agglutination titer ≥100 → suggests infection Note : Paul-Bunnell → sheep RBCs; Monospot → horse RBCs @Neet_pg_bot

with fever, sore throat, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly is classic for infectious mononucleosis (IM) caused by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV).

  • Diagnosis is supported by the Paul–Bunnell (Monospot) test, which detects heterophile IgM antibodies. These antibodies are non-specific and can agglutinate sheep or horse red blood cells—a hallmark of EBV infection.

    • Examples of Heterophile Antigen Tests:

    • Weil-Felix: Rickettsial infections

    • Paul-Bunnell: Infectious mononucleosis

    • Cold agglutination: Mycoplasma pneumonia

    • Streptococcus MG: Streptococcal antibodies

    Paul-Bunnell Test

    • Diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis caused by EBV.
    • Utilizes sheep RBCs as antigens to detect heterophile antibodies in the patient’s serum.

    • Principle: Heterophile antibodies agglutinate sheep RBCs; can occur rarely in normal individuals or after serum injections

    • Procedure: Heat serum (56°C, 30 min), mix with 1% sheep RBCs in doubling dilutions, incubate 37°C for 4 hrs

    • Interpretation: Agglutination titer ≥100 → suggests infection

    • Note: Paul-Bunnell → sheep RBCs; Monospot → horse RBCs

questions.solution: Femoral Neck Fractures Intracapsular Fractures (90%) These fractures occur within the joint capsule and affect the neck of the femur, which is enclosed by the hip joint's synovial membrane. Extracapsular Fractures (10%) These fractures occur outside the joint capsule, typically affecting areas below the neck of the femur, such as the trochanteric and subtrochanteric regions. Anatomical Classification of Intracapsular Fractures This classification focuses on the specific location within the femoral neck where the fracture occurs. It differentiates between fractures just below the femoral head and those at the base of the neck. Type Description Prognosis/Complications Subcapital Fracture just below the femoral head. Most common; high risk of avascular necrosis and nonunion. Transcervical Fracture through the midportion of the femoral neck. Intermediate risk of complications. Basicervical Fracture at the base of the femoral neck. Lower risk of avascular necrosis but transitions to extracapsular fractures. Garden’s Classification Garden’s classification is widely used to assess the completeness and displacement of femoral neck fractures. It also uses the trabecular alignment in radiographs to estimate the severity of the fracture. Grade Fracture Details Trabecular Alignment Prognosis Grade I Incomplete, valgus-impacted fracture. Normal trabecular alignment. Best prognosis. Grade II Complete, but without displacement. Normal trabecular alignment. Good prognosis with fixation. Grade III Complete with partial displacement. Misalignment between head and acetabulum. Increased risk of nonunion. Grade IV Complete with full displacement. Trabecular pattern parallel but displaced. Worst prognosis. High risk of avascular necrosis. @Neet_pg_bot

Femoral Neck Fractures


 

Intracapsular Fractures (90%)

These fractures occur within the joint capsule and affect the neck of the femur, which is enclosed by the hip joint's synovial membrane.

Extracapsular Fractures (10%)

These fractures occur outside the joint capsule, typically affecting areas below the neck of the femur, such as the trochanteric and subtrochanteric regions.


 

Anatomical Classification of Intracapsular Fractures

This classification focuses on the specific location within the femoral neck where the fracture occurs. It differentiates between fractures just below the femoral head and those at the base of the neck.



 

Type

Description

Prognosis/Complications

Subcapital

Fracture just below the femoral head.

Most common; high risk of avascular necrosis and nonunion.

Transcervical

Fracture through the midportion of the femoral neck.

Intermediate risk of complications.

Basicervical

Fracture at the base of the femoral neck.

Lower risk of avascular necrosis but transitions to extracapsular fractures.

Garden’s Classification

Garden’s classification is widely used to assess the completeness and displacement of femoral neck fractures. It also uses the trabecular alignment in radiographs to estimate the severity of the fracture.


 

Grade

Fracture Details

Trabecular Alignment

Prognosis

Grade I

Incomplete, valgus-impacted fracture.

Normal trabecular alignment.

Best prognosis.

Grade II

Complete, but without displacement.

Normal trabecular alignment.

Good prognosis with fixation.

Grade III

Complete with partial displacement.

Misalignment between head and acetabulum.

Increased risk of nonunion.

Grade IV

Complete with full displacement.

Trabecular pattern parallel but displaced.

Worst prognosis. High risk of avascular necrosis.

questions.answerText: It is a spinal reflex initiated by tapping the jaw.
questions.solution: he jaw jerk reflex is a deep tendon reflex with supraspinal involvement which is initiated by tapping the jaw. Masseter reflex or Jaw jerk reflex It is a deep tendon reflex. The reflex is initiated by tapping the midline of the mandible, which rapidly stretches the jaw-closing muscles (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid). The stretch activates muscle spindle afferents, which are sensory receptors in the muscles. Afferent pathway: Muscle spindle afferents → Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. Integration centre (Relay): Mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus. (Option B ruled out) Efferent pathway: Motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve → Mandibular nerve. (Option C ruled out) This results in the contraction of these jaw-closing muscles and finally closure of the jaw. The jaw jerk reflex is the only significant supraspinal monosynaptic reflex due to its relay in the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus. (Option D ruled out) The jaw jerk reflex can be tested in neurological examinations to assess the integrity of the trigeminal nerve and the brainstem pathways. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
he jaw jerk reflex is a deep tendon reflex with supraspinal involvement which is initiated by tapping the jaw.

 

Masseter reflex or Jaw jerk reflex

It is a deep tendon reflex.

  • The reflex is initiated by tapping the midline of the mandible, which rapidly stretches the jaw-closing muscles (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid).
  • The stretch activates muscle spindle afferents, which are sensory receptors in the muscles.
  • Afferent pathway: Muscle spindle afferents → Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
  • Integration centre (Relay): Mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus. (Option B ruled out)
  • Efferent pathway: Motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve → Mandibular nerve. (Option C ruled out)
  • This results in the contraction of these jaw-closing muscles and finally closure of the jaw.
  • The jaw jerk reflex is the only significant supraspinal monosynaptic reflex due to its relay in the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus. (Option D ruled out)
  • The jaw jerk reflex can be tested in neurological examinations to assess the integrity of the trigeminal nerve and the brainstem pathways.

questions.stem: What radiological feature distinguishes a sequestrum from living bone in a case of osteomyelitis?
questions.stemHtml: What radiological feature distinguishes a sequestrum from living bone in a case of osteomyelitis?
questions.solution: A sequestrum appears denser than the surrounding living bone on an X-ray because it is no longer involved in the normal bone remodelling or decalcification process. The lack of blood supply and ongoing inflammatory process preserve the mineral content, making it a bright, dense structure on imaging. Visually, they are pale in colour, with a smooth inner surface and a rough outer surface where surrounding tissue tries to erode it. Increased radiolucency (Option A): A sequestrum is denser and would appear brighter, not darker or more radiolucent, on an X-ray . Reduced density (Option B): Sequestra retain their density due to the lack of remodelling, so they appear denser, not less dense, than living bone. Fracture line (Option D): While a sequestrum can be separated from living bone, the appearance is typically characterized by increased density rather than a visible fracture line. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml:
A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency department with confusion, tremors, and diaphoresis. He has a long history of chronic alcohol use and has been drinking heavily for the past week. His family reports that he has not eaten well during this time. Upon examination, you note signs of malnutrition and his blood glucose level is found to be 50 mg/dL.
Which of the following statements regarding the effects of chronic alcoholism on nutritional deficiencies and blood glucose levels is FALSE?

options.label: A
options.text: Chronic alcohol use can cause vitamin B12 deficiency despite normal blood levels.

options.label: B
options.text: Folate deficiency in alcoholics leads to megaloblastic anemia.

options.label: C
options.text: Chronic alcohol use causes hypoglycemia by increasing the NADH/NAD+ ratio.

options.label: D
options.text: Chronic alcohol use causes hypoglycemia by decreasing the NADH/NAD+ ratio.

questions.answerText: Chronic alcohol use causes hypoglycemia by decreasing the NADH/NAD+ ratio.
questions.solution: Correct answer : D) Chronic alcohol use causes hypoglycemia by decreasing the NADH/NAD+ ratio. Chronic alcohol use and metabolism: Alcohol metabolism increases the NADH/NAD+ ratio, shifting metabolic pathways. Excess NADH promotes the conversion of pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, depleting key gluconeogenic precursors. This inhibits gluconeogenesis, leading to hypoglycemia, especially in malnourished individuals. The false statement is Option D , which states that alcohol decreases the NADH/NAD+ ratio, which is incorrect . Alcohol-Induced Metabolic Effects and Nutritional Deficiencies Effect Mechanism Increased NADH/NAD+ Ratio (Option C ruled out) Alcohol metabolism (via alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase) generates excess NADH, disrupting metabolic pathways. Hypoglycemia (Option C ruled out) Excess NADH inhibits gluconeogenesis, contributing to hypoglycemia. Pyruvate and oxaloacetate are diverted to lactate and malate, depleting gluconeogenic substrates. Lactic Acidosis Excess NADH promotes pyruvate to lactate conversion. Vitamin B12 Deficiency (Option A ruled out) Alcohol impairs B12 absorption despite normal blood levels. Folate Deficiency (Option B ruled out) Alcohol interferes with folate absorption and storage, leading to megaloblastic anemia. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct answer : D) Chronic alcohol use causes hypoglycemia by decreasing the NADH/NAD+ ratio.

  • Chronic alcohol use and metabolism:

    • Alcohol metabolism increases the NADH/NAD+ ratio, shifting metabolic pathways.

    • Excess NADH promotes the conversion of pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, depleting key gluconeogenic precursors.

    • This inhibits gluconeogenesis, leading to hypoglycemia, especially in malnourished individuals.

    • The false statement is Option D, which states that alcohol decreases the NADH/NAD+ ratio, which is incorrect.

Alcohol-Induced Metabolic Effects and Nutritional Deficiencies

Effect Mechanism
Increased NADH/NAD+ Ratio (Option C ruled out) Alcohol metabolism (via alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase) generates excess NADH, disrupting metabolic pathways.
Hypoglycemia (Option C ruled out) Excess NADH inhibits gluconeogenesis, contributing to hypoglycemia. Pyruvate and oxaloacetate are diverted to lactate and malate, depleting gluconeogenic substrates.
Lactic Acidosis Excess NADH promotes pyruvate to lactate conversion.
Vitamin B12 Deficiency (Option A ruled out) Alcohol impairs B12 absorption despite normal blood levels.
Folate Deficiency (Option B ruled out) Alcohol interferes with folate absorption and storage, leading to megaloblastic anemia.

Carotid space Around the contents of carotid sheath, demarcated by parts of investing, pretracheal, and prevertebral layers. Parapharyngeal space (Option A): While this space is adjacent to the pharynx and can be a site of infection, it does not communicate directly with the mediastinum. Carotid space (Option B): This space contains the carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve but is not typically involved in spreading infections to the mediastinum. questions.solutionHtml:
tomMeta" data-dictid="a5c6cb079d16927771967e62ffee72">posterior mediastinum. Infections in this space can easily spread to the mediastinum, leading to mediastinitis.

 

Classification of Spaces:

  • Suprahyoid spaces: Located above the hyoid bone, including the submandibular and prevertebral spaces.
  • Infrahyoid spaces: Located below the hyoid bone, typically related to deeper neck structures.

 

Suprahyoid spaces:

 

Submental space
  • Deep to upper investing layer of deep cervical fascia, superficial to mylohyoid muscles

Submandibular space
  • Deep to the concerned half of the mandible, between the anterior and posterior bellies of the digastric muscle

Sublingual space
  • Deep to mylohyoid muscles in the floor of the mouth, continuous with the opposite side

Peritonsillar space
  • Part of intrapharyngeal space, around palatine tonsils between pillars of fauces

Parapharyngeal space
  • On either side of the posterolateral aspect of pharynx
  • Medially - superior constrictor of pharynx
  • Laterally - medial pterygoid

Retropharyngeal space
  • Anteriorly - buccopharyngeal fascia of pharynx
  • Posteriorly - prevertebral layer
  • Laterally - carotid sheath
  • Superiorly - cranial base

 

Infrahyoid Spaces:

 

Pretracheal space
  • Behind pretracheal fascia and infrahyoid muscles, in front of the anterior wall of esophagus.

Retrovisceral space
  • Between the posterior wall of pharynx/esophagus and prevertebral fascia.

Prevertebral space
  • Between prevertebral fascia and vertebral column.

Carotid space
  • Around the contents of carotid sheath, demarcated by parts of investing, pretracheal, and prevertebral layers.

Parapharyngeal space (Option A): While this space is adjacent to the pharynx and can be a site of infection, it does not communicate directly with the mediastinum.
 

Carotid space (Option B): This space contains the carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve but is not typically involved in spreading infections to the mediastinum.
 

Prevertebral space (Option D): Infections here can affect the vertebrae or muscles but are less likely to spread to the mediastinum compared to the retropharyngeal space.

The physician prescribes a directly acting cholinergic drug to stimulate her salivary glands. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate for treating her condition?
questions.solution: 45-year-old woman is now complaining of xerostomia. One popular medication used to promote salivation is pilocarpine. Pilocarpine acts on the M3 receptors on the lacrimal and salivary glands, leading to increased secretions. Amides/Alkaloids Clinical significance Pilocarpine (Option C) Pilocarpine hydrochloride is used to treat xerostomia that develops after head and neck radiation treatments or that is linked to Sjögren syndrome and impairs their ability to secrete secretions (saliva and lacrimal), used for the treatment of angle closure glaucoma. Cevimeline Cevimeline primarily stimulates the M1 and M3 receptors. Compared to pilocarpine, cevimeline may have fewer adverse effects and a long-lasting sialogogic impact on the salivary and lacrimal glands. Choline esters Clinical significance Acetylcholine ACh is used topically as a 1% solution into the eye to induce miosis during surgery, while it is rarely administered systemically. Methacholine (Option D) Inhaling methacholine can diagnose bronchial airway hyperreactivity in patients without asthma symptoms. Bethanechol (Option B) GI and urinary tracts are the main organs affected by bethanechol. Bethanechol is useful for treating postop urine retention, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, and other chronic hypotonic, myogenic, or neurogenic bladder conditions when the organic blockage is absent. It can also be used to treat insufficient bladder emptying. Carbachol (Option A) Carbachol is injected into the eye as a 0.01% to 3% solution and is used topically in ophthalmology to treat glaucoma and induce miosis during surgery. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: According to Eugen Bleuler, which of the following symptoms are diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia? Affect disturbances Association disturbances Autism Ambivalence
questions.stemHtml:
According to Eugen Bleuler, which of the following symptoms are diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia?
	Affect disturbances
	Association disturbances
	Autism
	Ambivalence
questions.solution: Correct Answer- D) 1, 2, 3, 4 According to Eugen Bleuler, the diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia include (4 ‘A’s): Affect (emotional expression) disturbances : Patients often exhibit diminished emotional expression, which can be observed through a lack of facial expressions and emotional responsiveness. Association (thought processes) disturbances: refers to disorganised thinking, where patients may form unusual or illogical connections in their thoughts, such as catastrophic beliefs about the world. Autism (social withdrawal) refers to detachment from reality, evident in patients who may appear silent around others and frequently engage in self-directed conversation. Types Primary Hypothermia : Caused by environmental cold exposure, such as cold air or water. Common in cold geographic areas but can also occur in mild climates. Secondary Hypothermia : Results from conditions that impair heat production or increase heat loss (e.g., trauma, burns, drug overdoses, endocrine disorders, CNS injury, or drug effects). Exaplanation:

  • This patient has hypothermia, characterized by a core body temperature of 29°C, leading to symptoms such as lethargy, dilated pupils, and bradycardia. This condition results from prolonged exposure to cold, affecting the body's ability to maintain normal temperature and function.
  • Osborn (J) waves are often present in hypothermic patients and can indicate the severity of the condition.

 

 

J waves seen in ECG

Hypothermia

Definition

Hypothermia is defined as a drop in core body temperature below 35°C, resulting in the failure to maintain homeostasis and affecting all organ systems.

Types
  • Primary Hypothermia: Caused by environmental cold exposure, such as cold air or water. Common in cold geographic areas but can also occur in mild climates.
  • Secondary Hypothermia: Results from conditions that impair heat production or increase heat loss (e.g., trauma, burns, drug overdoses, endocrine disorders, CNS injury, or drug effects).

Clinical Features

Mild Hypothermia (32-35°C / 90-95°F)

(Option A)

  • Symptoms: Hunger, nausea, fatigue, shivering, pale/dry skin, increased muscle tone, blood pressure, heart rate, and respiration.
  • Neurologic symptoms: Cognitive decline, memory impairment, ataxia, dysarthria.
  • Shivering may stop if energy stores are depleted (e.g., malnutrition).
  • Cold-induced diuresis due to peripheral vasoconstriction.

Moderate Hypothermia (28-32°C / 82-90°F)

(Option B)
  • Cognitive decline, lethargy, CNS depression (hyporeflexia, dilated pupils).
  • Shivering stops at 30-32°C.
  • Paradoxical undressing may occur.
  • Increased risk of atrial fibrillation, hypotension, bradycardia, bradypnea.

Severe Hypothermia (<28°C / <82°F)

(Option C)
  • Unresponsiveness, further decline in cerebral blood flow, hypotension, bradycardia, and cardiac output.
  • Risk of atrial, junctional dysrhythmias.
  • Pulmonary congestion, oliguria, and areflexia.
  • Potential for cardiorespiratory failure and death.

ECG Findings
  • Atrial Fibrillation: Most common arrhythmia in hypothermic patients.
  • Bradycardia: Seen in moderate to severe hypothermia, increasing the risk of ventricular arrhythmias.
  • QT Interval Prolongation: Due to slowed impulse conduction through potassium channels.
  • Osborn (J) Waves: Elevated J point, visible on ECG in the precordial leads, with wave height proportional to the degree of hypothermia.

    • Ivermectin

    Mechanism of Action

    Ivermectin immobilises affected organisms by inducing a tonic paralysis of the musculature, activating glutamate-gated Cl⁻ channels found only in invertebrates.
     

    Therapeutic Uses
    • DOC for onchocerciasis in adults and children ≥5 yrs old.
    • As effective as DEC for controlling lymphatic filariasis.
    • Preferred drug for treating human strongyloidiasis.
    • First-line treatment for cutaneous larva migrans caused by dog or cat hookworms.
    • Option for treating scabies and head lice.

    Adverse Effects
    • In filarial infection, causes a Mazzotti-like reaction to dying microfilariae.
    • Risk of permanent disability and encephalopathies in patients with heavy L. loa microfilaria (≥ 30,000 per mm of blood)

    Precautions and Contraindications
    • C/I in conditions with an impaired blood-brain barrier, such as African trypanosomiasis and meningitis, due to its effects on GABA receptors.
    • Not approved for children <15 kg, pregnant women, or lactating women.

    Other Information

    Pyrantel Pamoate

    (Option B)

    Depolarisation of muscle by opening non-selective cation channels in worms, leading to spastic paralysis.
    • 2nd line drug for Nematodes
    		  

    Piperazine

    (Option C)

    Opens - GABA-A Cl channel , hyperpolarizes muscle & causes flaccid paralysis.
    • To treat Ascariasis and Enterobius
    • C/I in renal disease and epilepsy.
    • Safe in pregnancy.

    Niclosamide

    (Option D)

    Calcium influx causing spastic muscle paralysis
    • 2nd line drug for cestodes.
    • Used to treat intestinal T. solium infections, especially with suspected neurocysticercosis.
